data.title: France draws up emergency measures as petrol panic-buying sweeps country
data.description:
France has rushed out emergency measures to tackle a looming fuel crisis, with diesel prices at record highs and forecourts running dry.

The cash-strapped French government announced €450m (£386m) of handouts and subsidies to households and businesses to deal with what Roland Lescure, the finance minister, called “a very difficult and unchosen situation”.

The measures include cash handouts to people who use a car for work, energy vouchers for low-income households, and zero-interest loans for fishermen, who blockaded ports last week in protest at rising fuel prices.

“We must continue to help our fellow citizens who are on the front line, who are working and whose fuel prices have increased sharply,” Mr Lescure told reporters.

Attacks by Iranian proxy forces on Saudi Arabia’s pipelines and coastline have disrupted oil supplies to Europe, driving petrol and diesel prices to the highest level since Donald Trump attacked Iran on Feb 28.

France’s diesel price averaged €2.42 a litre on Monday, up more than 10 cents in the past week. Unleaded petrol has jumped to €2.19 a litre.

Panic-buying has swept the country, leaving one fifth of French petrol stations short of at least one fuel type.

TotalEnergies forecourts, which cap prices at €2.25 a litre for diesel and €1.99 for petrol, are bearing the brunt of the shortages. Independent petrol stations have seen customer traffic drop between 20pc and 40pc, as motorists turn to Total.

Mr Lescure insisted there were “no supply problems”, but added: “We must prepare for a possible deterioration of the situation. ... Uncertainties remain high.”

The French government had already allowed fuel distributors to top up supplies to forecourts by selling “summer-blend diesel”, which is less cold-resistant, for two weeks beyond the usual Nov 1 cut-off.

Ministers have also extended previous support measures introduced in April until the end of the year. These subsidies, ranging from 15 to 35 cents a litre, target diesel-intensive sectors, such as agriculture, fisheries and construction.

That followed a wave of strikes and protests last week against rising fuel prices, including a blockade of French ports by irate French fishermen.

The government on Tuesday expanded its €100 grant to “high-mileage” drivers, those who commute more than nine miles each way between home and work or drive more than 5,000 miles a year for work.

Only half of eligible French motorists have claimed the cash so far, but the pool of eligible drivers has been widened from three million to 5.5 million.

The energy vouchers for low-income households will range from €48 to €277. Employers will be able to offer a fuel bonus of up to €1,000 to their workers, and rural nurses will be entitled to a separate €80 bonus.

The promise of yet more support comes amid France’s ongoing battle to get public spending under control.

Mr Lescure said he would not be cutting excise duties on petrol, adding that a 20-cent cut would cost the public purse almost €10bn.

He has already admitted that the budget deficit will remain stuck above 5pc this year, and the government’s debt-to-GDP ratio will swell to a record 119pc.

An election to choose a successor to Emmanuel Macron, the president, in April 2027 is pressuring politicians to spend more to shore up the economy and ease voters’ pain.

Germany has demanded an EU-wide windfall tax on oil companies’ profits to help pay for national governments’ cuts to fuel duties.

Mr Macron wrote to Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, on Friday demanding that Brussels also take action to support business and motorists.

In a letter reported in the French media on Tuesday, he said the EU should relax fuel standards on kerosene and diesel, which would help oil refineries turn crude into fuel more quickly.

He also called for more biofuel blending into diesel, and said Brussels should postpone new methane-emission rules on oil and gas importers.

data.title: Thousands of homes no longer subject to bats and newts rules
data.description:
Housing developers will no longer need to seek approval for new homes from Natural England, putting an end to the prospect of bats and newts holding up routine planning applications.

Natural England, the environmental quango, had been required to examine more than 22,000 planning applications for new developments annually.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, last year criticised nature rules for prioritising the needs of wildlife such as “bats and newts” over new developments.

She said: “As a country, we’ve cared more about the bats than we have about the commuter times for people in Leeds and West Yorkshire, and we’ve got to change that.”

The body has been criticised for its excessive caution in its consultation responses, holding up planning applications. Some of its rules have resulted in a de facto ban on new residential construction in several areas across England because of worries about water pollution.

Natural England was also criticised after it was consulted on a £100m “bat tunnel”, constructed over the High Speed 2 railway, and for its advice on a £700m underwater sound system – dubbed the “fish disco” – at the Hinkley Point C nuclear power station.

Legislation had required Natural England to reply to all large-scale planning applications, irrespective of whether they were a risk to the environment or not.

The environmental body could answer “no comment” to proposals that it felt did not require its engagement. However, this led to a large number of consultations where planning applications were registered and replied to with a “no comment” response.

New guidance means that councils will be able to rely on pre-written advice on whether they should seek input from Natural England, and they will be able to wave through more routine developments without consulting the quango.

The reforms will allow the environmental watchdog to focus on responding to planning proposals “which present the greatest risks or opportunities for nature”.

The changes mean Natural England will shift away from offering repeated advice on individual planning applications and instead provides more tailored advice for larger-scale projects.

The Government hopes this will speed up the planning application process for thousands of new developments as Labour races to accelerate housebuilding across the country.

Neil Hornby, the chief executive of Natural England, said: “This change of approach will help us focus our expertise where it can have the greatest impact for nature, while supporting efficient decision making across the planning system.

“Natural England is laser focused on advancing nature recovery and meeting key legal Environment Act targets, while supporting the Government’s ambition for good growth in every postcode.”

data.title: Greggs to axe hundreds of jobs after replacing humans with robots
data.description:
Greggs has put hundreds of workers at risk of redundancy after unveiling plans to shut four factories and replace staff with automated machinery.

The bakery chain said 740 jobs could go between now and 2028 as part of a plan to change where it makes its food.

Greggs will start installing more automated machinery instead of relying on its workforce at the sites, making the existing factories redundant.

It said the changes, which would take place over two and a half years, were needed to make sure it could keep up with demand as the business grows.

The proposals are expected to result in four manufacturing sites closing, while some other sites will stop making food but continue to be used for distribution.

Greggs said it was also considering moving some packing operations into sites it already owns.

The company has started a consultation with affected workers and trade unions. A decision is expected towards the end of November.

The announcement came as Greggs reported a 7.7pc rise in sales in the three months to the end of September, with like-for-like sales up 3.4pc.

The stronger performance, helped by new products including its steak-and-Stilton bake and iced drinks, led Greggs to raise its expectations for profits this year.

Shares in Greggs were up 6pc on Wednesday morning after the announcement.

It has opened 95 shops this year, taking its total to 2,796. It expects to open up to 15 additional shops by the end of 2026.

Roisin Currie, the Greggs chief executive, said: “This is really about Greggs making themselves fit for the future. As we become a stronger growing business, then there are opportunities to consolidate.”

Greggs is also spending heavily on two new sites in Derby and in Kettering, Northamptonshire, which will help it supply more shops as the business grows.

The Derby site will start to operate this year while the Kettering site is set to open in 2027. Greggs said the two sites would eventually give it enough capacity to supply at least 3,500 shops.

The new sites will also use more machinery to move and sort food. At Derby, machinery will handle frozen food, while Kettering will use it to move chilled and room-temperature food around the site.

Greggs said the new sites would make its food-making and delivery network more efficient, although they would increase its costs next year before beginning to save money.

The company warned that there were also signs costs would rise more quickly in 2027.

Greggs said about half of its energy costs for next year had already been hedged but warned that higher energy and diesel prices could eventually feed through into the cost of ingredients such as fertiliser, crops and protein.

Greggs said the four proposed closures would cost about £60m, including £40m spent on the changes themselves, as well as the cost of closing the sites and making workers redundant.

Once the changes are complete, Greggs expects them to save about £20m a year.

The savings are expected to come through in 2028 and 2029.

The job cuts follow a strong first half for Greggs. Sales rose 7.2pc to £1.1bn in the six months to June, while pre-tax profits jumped almost 20pc to £76m.

Ms Currie said Greggs would try to find alternative jobs within the business for affected workers where possible, with the company already looking at vacancies in the areas where the factories are based.

data.title: Reform drums up business support at conference
data.description:
Large firms are flocking to Reform UK’s national conference as the party prepares to host its inaugural business day.

First Bus, BT, Vodafone, Google, Heathrow, JCB, Dubai Ports and TikTok are among the businesses sponsoring or running events at the three-day summit which starts on Thursday in Birmingham.

The party’s decision to host a business day forms part of a wider Reform UK strategy to replace the Conservatives as the main opposition party to Andy Burnham’s government by fighting Labour on economic grounds.

In recent weeks, the party has unveiled plans for the biggest welfare shake-up “in a generation” by scrapping key benefits to save £50bn a year, more than double what the Tories plan to save, as well as pledging a £30 rebate for taxpayers stuck on hold to His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs (HMRC).

To appeal to wealthy backers, they are also offering conference packages worth up to £3,000, which include a champagne breakfast with Nigel Farage, an opportunity to meet and network with senior Reform leaders and a three-course meal in the Platinum hospitality area.

‘Increased engagement’

The party has toned down its offerings from last year in an attempt to professionalise, scrapping offers of custom cocktail naming rights and the delivery of bottles of sparkling wine to business stands.

A Reform UK spokesman told The Telegraph: “Engagement from British business has increased significantly. Companies across the country recognise they need to understand Reform and what a future Reform government could mean for them.

“Businesses now realise that the possibility of a Reform government is very real and are acting accordingly.”

Until 2025, Reform had a relatively low attendance from big business compared with similar events organised by Labour and the Tories.

But the influx of big business to this year’s annual event signals that the corporate world is taking the possibility of a Reform government seriously, as the party continues to outperform rivals in voter intention polling.

Crypto sidelined

Reform, which topped polls for almost 16 consecutive months between March 2025 and July 2026 and won hundreds of councillors in May, is now in second place trailing the Labour Party following a so-called Burnham bounce.

Meanwhile, Mr Farage is also believed to be sidelining crypto companies in favour of mainstream corporates following a backlash over the Reform leader’s £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, the Bitcoin billionaire.

Crypto companies are not among the businesses sponsoring the 2026 conference, which last year included donations from crypto payments firm Zebec.

The party has also scrapped perks it had previously offered to crypto industry leaders, including free tickets and access to senior figures, according to City AM, in a notable departure from previous years.

Conferences and the sponsorship fees that come in from big businesses are one of the ways that political parties raise revenue for their campaigning efforts.

A Heathrow spokesman said the airport had “a long history of constructive engagement across the political spectrum”.

He said: “Like many businesses – from airlines to pubs and banks to supermarkets – it is common practice to sponsor events at party conferences to engage policymakers and ensure they better understand the needs of consumers and the economy.”

data.title: The rise and fall of British helicopters
data.description:
Do you have a favourite helicopter? Mine, as a child, was Airwolf. But it could have been the helicopter that dropped Anneka Rice off at so many castles in the pioneering 1980s Channel 4 game-show Treasure Hunt, or the Blue Thunder choppers that ferry our elite SAS teams around Britain, tackling emergencies.

Today, in addition to their use by armed forces, they are status symbols for the 0.01 per cent. Donald Trump used to owned a fleet of three Sikorsky S-76 helicopters, with predictably gilded interiors. Yet not so long ago, some believed this form of transport would be used regularly by the hoi polloi; hopping into a chopper would be as common as hailing a black cab.

This month marks 40 years since the demise of British Airways Helicopters, and that brief moment in time when it seemed scheduled passenger helicopter services might actually catch on. So why did the helicopter never go truly mainstream?

Up in the Airlink

Focke-Wulf’s FW61 was unveiled in the 1930s, before Russian-American pioneer Igor Sikorsky took up the baton in the 1940s. The US company he founded would go on to dominate these machines’ development for half a century.

But passenger helicopter services actually began in the UK. The route? From Liverpool to Cardiff, launched by BEA in 1950, with an intriguing stop in Wrexham that would have suited Rob McElhenney and Ryan Reynolds if it were operating today.

More BEA routes followed, such as Birmingham to Northolt, and on to Heathrow. Birmingham got a pioneering “Rotorstation” for helicopters to land at. It was opened at Heybarnes Recreation Ground in Hay Mills – Peaky Blinders territory. Three flights left for London daily.

Between 1978 and 1986, a helicopter shuttle service, dubbed the Airlink, connected Gatwick and Heathrow. This was before the M25 was finished and when the journey between the two main London airports was tortuous. Helicopters ferried transit passengers from apron to apron in minutes.

A vision of the future

The thinking among many was that helicopters would be omnipresent. During the Festival of Britain, there was a helicopter landing pad on the Southbank in London. The Southbank was earmarked for a more permanent heliport, which explains the brutalist design of the Queen Elizabeth Hall. It was supposed to protect against the noise and vibrations of helicopters.

In the end a heliport at Battersea was opened, further along the River Thames, and is still in use today. Architects’ designs for Sixties new towns always showed two things: a monorail, and helicopters fluttering in the sky. This was the vision of the future – back when we believed in a future that would be better.

Even the GPO became enamoured with helicopters and trialled their use to deliver post to the rural towns of Norfolk. Quite what Farmer Giles, drinking a pint of warm Bullard’s outside The Railway Inn in Docking on a Sunday afternoon in 1948, would have made of the sight of a GPO Sikorsky S-51 on a post run to Wells-Next-The-Sea is anyone’s guess.

In the Fifties, Britain ramped up its own helicopter production at Westland’s Yeovil site, which became the home of the British helicopter. The Dragonfly, Widgeon, Whirlwind and Wessex became instantly recognisable machines built in Somerset. The Sea King, Wasp and Scout followed, then it was into the era of more modern machines like the Puma, Gazelle and Lynx.

Away with the Faireys

Among the more bizarre ideas was the Fairey Rotodyne: a hybrid between a plane and a helicopter that doesn’t look a million miles away from the stretched fuselage of the Chinook. In 1959 it flew from Heathrow to Paris via Dover and Brussels, but it wouldn’t catch on. One of the problems was the immense noise its rotors generated. This was going to be a problem when it was clattering over the roofs of densely populated areas of South London on the way to Battersea Heliport.

Westland took over Fairey in the 1960s, but domestic helicopter production was to become a hot political potato. Britain’s varied and incredibly successful aerospace entities were walking a tightrope between innovating, investing, exporting and balancing the books. Their designs were legendary, but of course not everything worked. There was always a tussle between nationalising everything into what would become British Aerospace and selling parts off to foreign investors.

Westland became a political football during the so-called Westland Affair in 1985, which pitted different factions of Margaret Thatcher’s Conservative government against each other, as arguments raged over whether to maintain this facility in Yeovil, who should run it and who would pay for it.

End of an era

Why did helicopters fade away? As with other futuristic transport ideas like hovertrains, monorails, hovercraft and other “gadgetbahns”, their relatively high cost and niggling technical problems could never be fully resolved.

Aeroplanes, trains and cars driving on motorways won the transport arms race because they could be easily scaled, and eventually mass uptake drastically reduced costs. These forms of transport made money rather than costing it.

Motorways connect us. With the M40 complete, there was no need to take a helicopter from Birmingham to London. Helicopters are also gas guzzlers – even Porsche owners would baulk at the price of a full tank. Sabena wanted to follow the Rotodyne’s first international flight and start a helicopter from London to Brussels – but Eurostar does that journey more efficiently.

In the US, where traffic is terrible and public transport is worse, Blade has put up a fight, offering relatively affordable flights from JFK to Manhattan, but without the drama of the former Pan Am helicopter, which whisked passengers to the top of the Pan Am HQ in Midtown in the 1960s.

Helicopters are still popular as niche forms of transport, and incredibly useful for medical evacuations, police and military use, and VIP transport. UK Air Sea Rescue has used helicopters to rescue the lives of countless sailors around our shores, and helicopters have ferried thousands of workers to oil and gas rigs in the North Sea and beyond, from Aberdeen, Norwich, Humberside and other hubs.

But their mass-market use has dwindled in the face of competition – which is sad, because they have a real value. The experience of being in one is not like regular flying because you’re so low you can see everything below you. The feeling of rising into the sky for the first time is surreal.

Rare survivors

The Scilly Isles are one of the rare examples of a route where helicopters make sense, and these flights have continued on and off from 1964 to this day. My honeymooning parents cannot have been the only holidaymakers caught out by rough seas who needed to use the helicopter as a way to swiftly get off the islands. For locals, they are a lifeline back to the shops, schools and health services of Penzance. This is now the last surviving scheduled British helicopter service.

Nice to Monaco and Saint-Tropez are other popular services going strong, as are Helity’s routes from Malaga and Algeciras to the headline-grabbing Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Hong Kong to Macau is another example. Faroese flag carrier Atlantic Airways runs domestic helicopter flights. But anyone who’s gone puffin-spotting in Mykines, and found themselves stuck on the island for days due to bad weather, will know that helicopters aren’t much use in storms or low visibility, which is pretty much every day in a Faroe Islands winter.

For the super-rich class there will always be helicopters ready to take them to the British Grand Prix or Goodwood (two of the biggest weekends for the Battersea Heliport). But for the rest of us, the dream of flying everywhere by helicopter is elusive. It’s not impossible though – this is why helicopter aficionados specifically head to Tresco or Tórshavn.

data.title: Airlines banned from charging parents to sit next to their children
data.description:
Airlines will be banned from charging parents extra to sit with their children on flights.

The Government has proposed a set of rules requiring airlines to seat children under the age of 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge.

According to the Department for Transport, it can cost a parent up to £104 to arrange to sit next to their child on a return journey.

Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking to correct a mistake.

It is thought ministers will bring in the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays.

MPs are debating a new set of rules for travel companies as the Civil Aviation (Consumer Protection and Regulatory Reform) Bill makes its way through Parliament.

The proposed law will give ministers powers to draw up a list of passenger rights and a list of duties which both airlines and airports must undertake.

‘Giving people room to breathe’

Andy Burnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either.

“People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them.

“This is what our everyday fixes are all about – giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.”

Rory Boland, the editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together.

“Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.”

Earlier this year, Ryanair adjusted its family seating policy after an investigation was launched into the company charging parents to sit with their children on flights.

The Irish operator previously required parents travelling with children between two and 11 years old to pay to reserve what it referred to as a mandatory family seat. Children were then allocated seats next to or near parents free of charge.

The fee for a mandatory family seat was typically about £8 each way, the UK Competition and Markets Authority found.

At the time, Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair, said its previous policy was “the most progressive and transparent in Europe”.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, has also announced a crackdown on bad behaviour by passengers on aircraft, with the Government, airlines and trade unions working on a system to share information about disruptive passengers.

Airlines logged more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents in 2025, government figures show, including what it described as a mid-air brawl that caused a flight to be diverted.

Using the information-sharing system, airlines could choose to ban persistently disruptive passengers from their aircraft.

“Everyone deserves to travel knowing their flight isn’t going to be disrupted by bad behaviour from a small minority,” Ms Alexander said.

“These common-sense reforms will make flying safer for staff and passengers and protect people from unnecessary charges, whoever they fly with.”

data.title: Beware the rise of AI shopping assistants
data.description:
Find me the cheapest pair of Ugg boots for under £200, or a bean-to-cup coffee machine for under £300. Switch my broadband supplier when the price drops to £25 for gigabit. I’m going to the pub, dear computer, so can you do it all for me?

Robots will do the hard work in the world of AI agentic commerce, finding bargains, negotiating prices and making purchases. The tireless AI never sleeps.

This future came a little closer last week as Meta launched Muse, a personal AI agent promising to do your shopping and more. Muse can follow instructions and even make phone calls on your behalf – answering your security questions – and wait while you’re put on hold. Who wouldn’t want all that hassle removed from their lives?

The fly in the ointment of consumer capitalism is the friction suppliers throw in our way. A whole arsenal of devious tools is deployed. Finding the best deal on a train ticket could be a PhD subject in itself. Ofcom gave Virgin Media a record fine earlier this year for making it so hard for customers to leave. Friction is a customer-retention strategy.

Ronald Coase, the Nobel Prize-winning economist, spent his career thinking about this. Markets don’t work as well as they could when the cost of a transaction is considered to outweigh the benefits, he noted.

After 30 years of the web, we should be a lot closer to Coase’s utopia of perfect markets: information is abundant, and new suppliers are just a click away. But we’re no closer to solving the problem, and I have a theory about why.

Forty years ago, information was much harder to find, but most British households had one breadwinner, not two. That meant one person could devote more time to finding the right information.

Today, we all have much less time to make a decision.

“The frictions disproportionately affect households with less time, confidence or capacity to engage, contributing to poorer outcomes (especially for vulnerable consumers) and potentially reduced trust in markets,” the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) noted this year.

One sarcastic reaction to Muse said that it would be adopted by “people who would like to spend twenty to a hundred dollars a month to be a middle manager of their own lives”, but that missed the point. A lot of us would like the agents to work. However, the problems we are putting them up against are not trivial to solve.

It’s a legal minefield, for one thing, as two academics found last year in a much-cited paper. Queen Mary’s Garry Gabison and UC Berkeley’s Patrick Xian applied Principal Agent Theory, which examines conflicts that can arise when an agent acts on behalf of others and concluded that today’s AI fell far short of real-world readiness.

“LLM agents cannot satisfy all criteria of a normal agent, creating an agency gap that can lead to an excess of unpredictable actions,” they wrote.

In practice, for example, an agreement doesn’t mean an agreement, as an agent can’t be considered “rational”, so a contract can’t be valid. And AI agents perform worse as problems become more complex.

This week, a study of bots found they gave the wrong financial advice much of the time and collapsed when faced with multi-part advice. The accuracy rate fell from a poor 43pc to 12pc, according to the Saturn “Artificial Authority” report.

Consider how many individual steps and judgments a simple transaction requires. You need those new boots for someone’s birthday. Will they arrive in time? The merchant’s bot is offering your AI a better deal on that coffee machine, but it has a lower capacity. Should your bot accept the offer?

Consumers won’t be the only ones using AI agents. The suppliers will too: bots will be battling bots. Gabison and Xian also described how liability becomes a minefield when lots of bots are running in “multi-agent systems”. If you receive a bad deal, who or what is at fault?

In a world full of robot dealmakers, it’s only natural for producers to want to collude. In March, the CMA flagged that it was watching for “coordinated outcomes and higher prices” caused by the adoption of AI in e-commerce. This could happen without intent, it noted, and warned merchants not to use the same pricing recommendations as their rivals.

Amazon recently reminded us of the power a dominant player can use when faced with a Coasian threat: within hours of Muse’s launch last week, Amazon blocked Meta’s agents from using the site to browse or buy stuff. Only a feisty competition regulator can force change in cases like this. (Note how when switching broadband and mobile services, you don’t have to contact the service you are leaving at all. They didn’t do that voluntarily but because regulators had made them.)

Finally, we should remember that anything turned into software becomes more vulnerable to attack or manipulation. Blockchain “smart contracts”, fashionable a few years ago, replaced a middleman with a programmable piece of software triggered by an event, akin to the world of high-frequency trading. But events in this market show the risks of leaving it all to the computers.

Two “flash crashes” in 2010 and 2015 saw dramatic falls in equity values for a few minutes, one wiping $1tn (£750bn) off shares. Both were attributed to a self-taught trader thousands of miles away, working from his bedroom in Hounslow.

AI enthusiasts like to call their new tool a “force multiplier”. But agentic commerce could very quickly become a “farce multiplier” instead. Rather than simply securing the best deal, we could end up with more headaches. This is regrettable. We could all benefit from markets that work better and remove friction for consumers.

data.title: Christmas in September is a surefire way to kill any excitement
data.description:
Four thousand people booked their Ocado Christmas delivery slots last Thursday – and that was just between 12am (when they were first released) and 1am.

This makes me feel two things in quick succession. First, who are these absolute freaks? What kind of a person sits there at 11:55pm on a warm September day frenziedly adding a list of Christmas foodstuffs (that they will already have itemised in an Excel spreadsheet) to their cart? Second, maybe I should start frenziedly adding random Christmas foodstuffs to my cart? What if they run out of slots? What if they run out of pigs in blankets? How does one even compile an Excel spreadsheet?

There are, of course, two small problems. I don’t know where I’m spending Christmas yet, let alone whether I’ll be cooking lunch. Oh, and I’m allergic to everything about the grotesque consumerist delirium that seems to infect us all at the mere mention of the “C” word.

As a child, I loved Christmas because it was relaxed – and to me, that is synonymous with joy. In fact, nothing that isn’t relaxed can be even remotely joyful. My brothers and I stayed in our pyjamas all day. Yes, we put away gargantuan quantities of food, but I don’t remember there being canapés, formal courses and precisely the right side dishes – or any stress about the redcurrant jelly having expired at some point during the Harold Wilson government.

Gifts, likewise, were low-key to inconsequential. One year, my older brother took five Agatha Christies (that I’d already read) off the sitting room bookshelves, wrapped them up and presented them to me.

When that’s your baseline, today’s Christmas hysteria is impossible to get used to. While I’m all for the three P’s (prior planning and preparation), it seems to have become a competitive sport in the build-up to Christmas. This build-up is starting earlier and earlier, leaching all joy from that most joyous of days.

Any minute now, some small-talk maker will ask whether I’ve “finished my Christmas shopping”, and my reply will be the same one I’ve given for the past 20 years. “No, I like to do it all late afternoon on Christmas Eve.” The sheen of sweat on their brow and the palpable panic – I’d be lying if I said I didn’t enjoy it.

On the subject of panic, according to John Lewis, online searches for Christmas from customers “getting into the festive spirit” were up 193 per cent in May and June from the same time last year. Meanwhile, Ocado has gleefully informed us that 52 per cent of all the Christmas stuff they’ll sell this year will already be in customers’ baskets by tomorrow.

I should think so. They’re going to need to start stockpiling those Easter eggs at midnight on Thursday, aren’t they?

data.title: Tory donor Lord Ashcroft takes stake in troubled Mirror publisher
data.description:
Billionaire Tory donor Lord Ashcroft has taken a stake in the struggling publisher behind the Mirror and Express newspapers.

The British businessman has taken a 3pc stake in Reach, worth around £4.4m, through his investment vehicle Heather Venture Holdings.

Alex deGroote, a media analyst, said Lord Ashcroft, the former deputy chairman of the Conservative Party, may attempt to seek influence over Reach’s strategy.

But he also described the investment as “shrewd” bargain hunting after a slump in the publisher’s share price to just 47p.

The company now has a market value of less than £150m – a fraction of its £5bn peak in 2005.

The move will add to Lord Ashcroft’s existing media holdings, which include news brands such as Politics Home and Conservative Home, as well as Biteback Publishing.

The 80-year-old life peer, who has written for the Daily Express, is also the majority shareholder in Gusbourne, the English sparkling wine producer, and has a major stake in data science company Jaywing.

Lord Ashcroft’s swoop comes at a torrid time for Reach, which also owns scores of local titles including the Manchester Evening News and Liverpool Echo.

The publisher unveiled plans this month to cut a further 220 journalists as it grapples with a sharp downturn in reader numbers. It also said it will shutter three of its online news outlets in Kent, Aberdeen and Galway.

Reach also axed more than 300 editorial roles in a cost-cutting round last year.

Reach has been paying the price for its strategy of chasing clicks as digital advertising revenues have shrunk and the rise of AI summaries has diverted readers away from news sites.

In July, the company said its Google referrals had plunged by 55pc in the first half of the year, triggering a 9pc fall in revenues. Reach reported a pre-tax loss of £45m.

Piers North, chief executive of Reach, has since pledged to reverse the newspaper group’s paywall-free strategy and focus instead on generating subscription revenues directly from readers.

Reach has around 40,000 paid subscribers and bosses have pointed to “active engaged time” as the most important metric, rather than page views.

The London-listed company is currently searching for a new chairman as incumbent Nick Prettejohn prepares to step down ahead of next year’s annual general meeting.

This month it appointed Clive Whiley, chairman of Scottish broadcaster STV, to its board. Mr Whiley, who was previously chairman of banknote printer De La Rue, is considered a frontrunner to take up the role.

Reach declined to comment. Lord Ashcroft has been contacted for comment.

data.title: My money-savvy mother was scammed out of £2.1m after her Alzheimer’s diagnosis
data.description:
Before her diagnosis of Alzheimer’s at 60, my mother had always been great with money. She was a fiercely independent finance director of a global company, who had been quietly saving for her retirement and my grandmother’s care.

She certainly wasn’t a big spender. Our grandparents took us away rather than mum so she could work, and she never bought anything unnecessary or flashy.

She was a young 60 too, diligently going to her Pilates classes every morning and aiming to sign up to complete her 10th Ironman triathlon with me. She was even travelling with work in Japan the month before her diagnosis.

Today, she is scared to leave the house without letting me know first and needs encouragement to use her debit card. She is worried about how it works and about spending money.

She just doesn’t believe she can do anything any more. She still volunteers in her local shop every day, but when I encourage her to do things, she says: “No, no, no! I’ll get it wrong. I’ve ruined all our lives.”

I’ll never forgive the scammers for what they took from her – and us as a family.

When the symptoms of Alzheimer’s first started to show, I thought my mother was just stressed. I assumed work and life had been weighing on her. My grandfather had recently died and that had affected the whole family. But she soon started to lose track of the time and at that point she moved in with me in Manchester so I could take control of the situation.

She started regularly going out on midnight wanders and when I confronted her she would say she was late for work or Pilates – even though it would be pitch black outside.

At the time, my brother and I (we were 26 and 29) made light of the situation. We had no idea what was happening, and we didn’t for a moment consider Alzheimer’s could be the cause. She was only 59.

The turning point came on my 30th birthday. She arrived wearing her pyjamas and said she had booked a flight for that night from Luton airport but had locked herself out of her phone and didn’t know the way. It was all so bizarre and worrying.

We took her to the GP and, after much back and forth, she was finally referred to a memory assessment centre. And then quite unexpectedly we received the young-onset Alzheimer’s diagnosis on June 13, 2025.

That weekend, we were out for lunch when I saw someone saved in her phone as “financial manager” had texted her, which I thought was really odd. She had never mentioned a manager before, nor had she ever needed financial advice.

I took her phone discreetly and read the chats under the table. It became clear that my mother had been persuaded to take out a string of loans. When we got home, we went through her accounts and I realised she had been regularly sending hundreds of thousands of pounds from her bank account.

I called Report Fraud there and then. I didn’t know what to do. I was in shock. I spent all of that Saturday in a panic, calling the banks and trying to get her locked out of her accounts.

The next day, I caught her on the phone again with another scammer. Someone had messaged her saying she owed them £200,000 and she wrote back: “I’m trying, but HSBC won’t let me. I’m so sorry. I owe you money. I need to fix that quickly.” Everything seemed planned to play on her growing anxiety and worry about upsetting others.

I was furious. We went through her financial statements and on page after page there were at least two to three £50,000 payments. It was all so overwhelming. My mother was just sitting next to me silent as my brother and I combed through the papers. I think it was all dawning on her.

She shut down and wouldn’t speak to us about it. She just couldn’t explain what was going on, and she thought she was doing right for the family.

All in all, she had been scammed out of £2.1m – her entire life’s savings.

It transpired that she had been targeted by two scammers, who claimed to work for investment companies.

One ran a highly sophisticated operation, with a proper website which let us log on and see our mum’s transfers. I spoke to this man a few times, he was convincing, confident, and kept the story rolling until I said we would not be moving any more money. The second company also had a convincing accounts page but whenever we phoned up to ask why we couldn’t withdraw, we were told the scammer no longer worked for the company and had disappeared.

Mum also tried to take out 11 loans, five of which came through totalling £120,000. She was paying £2,500 a month for over a year. We were advised to keep repaying if we could and we couldn’t afford to be chased by debt collectors on top of everything else.

Once we discovered the scams, we set up power of attorney that week, and since then most of my time has been consumed by sorting this out.

I found all the emails she had been sending one of the scammers. She had confided in him, telling him of her own mother’s dementia diagnosis and the cost of her care. He assured her she would be making a good investment. When she told him of her own diagnosis, he was sympathetic at first, before asking her to send another £50,000.

Reading those emails is probably the saddest thing I’ve ever had to do. There were lots of photos of the dog and one of me finishing the half marathon. She was so clearly proud of me, even to a complete stranger. The scammer, of course, soon asked her for a picture of my ID and she sent him a picture of my passport.

Naively, I thought the police and banks would help us, and that it would all be sorted. The most I ever got from the authorities was an automated email and a cursory home visit telling us to contact Report Fraud.

I’ve never needed the police before, but I thought they would be interested in what was effectively the robbery of £2.1m. There is a person running around in the world somewhere with millions of pounds, while all the plans my mother had for herself went upside down. If they have managed this with my mum I worry how many other families this has affected too.

As for the banks, I thought they would have seen the almost twice-weekly transfers of £50,000 to a strange international account. I kept ringing and ringing but no one would engage. They’d say someone would contact me soon, but no one ever did.

I had nowhere to go and so I decided to enlist a private investigator to look into the scammers in October 2025. I paid them £3,000 and I thought I would be able to hand over their report to the police. I managed to send it to the banks, but I never managed to get it to the police – as much as I did try.

Eventually, HSBC gave us £455,000 as a gesture of goodwill, which is the maximum amount the Financial Ombudsman can make them pay us. I’ve still never spoken to anyone there. I received the payment from the ombudsman without further explanation, which is a life changing sum of money.

At first, I was quite embarrassed to talk about what happened with other people. The number – £2.1m – is staggering, and it felt embarrassing to acknowledge my mother had that much money in the first place. I had no idea that was the case, and I was worried others wouldn’t be as sympathetic. I hadn’t even told my closest friends about it until a couple of months ago.

So, when I overheard two friends dismissing what happened – on account of all the money she had – I felt really hurt. I remember thinking that this was why I was anxious to tell people. It was a complete lack of respect.

Lots of people, though, have been incredibly supportive. I’ve been really surprised, especially with friends that I wasn’t as close with, who would make plans – even if it was just for coffee – and ask me to bring my mother along. They’re amazing with her and it makes me feel so light in those moments. It allows her to still be herself, even if that is a different person to the one I knew.

Others have offered to take her to the shops or give her a lift to her regular doctor’s appointment. Most importantly, they treat her like a normal human being – and that’s made the biggest difference.

My friends and family want me to move on and have encouraged me to say that out loud. But inside, I feel so frustrated that a scam could happen again to anybody. I can’t believe no one’s after them. No one is even trying to chase them. That just can’t be.

A spokesman for HSBC UK said: “We’re sorry to hear about any reports of scams or fraud and of the customer’s Alzheimer’s diagnosis following this scam. We’re pleased this case has since been resolved, following discussions with our customer and the Financial Ombudsman Service.”

As told to Erik Olsson.

data.title: Interactive Investor offers financial advice for £100 a month – but is it worth it?
data.description:
Many of us know we could probably benefit from financial advice, but 91pc don’t take it, according to the Financial Conduct Authority.

It’s a startling figure, but it isn’t without reason. Advice fees can be expensive and the profession is no stranger to bad press.

However, with the rising prevalence of online “finfluencers” and AI chatbots, the financial regulator is keen to change the landscape with more affordable and accessible advice.

Enter Aberdeen’s Interactive Investor (ii). From £100 a month (£150 for couples), ii Advice will provide you with a personalised financial plan, along with ongoing support from a financial adviser.

The price tag is certainly eye-catching – but is it worth paying for?

What’s on offer

You can pick one of seven remote financial advisers for a free introductory video call, and then arrange calls as often as you’d like, with at least one annual review. You can swap advisers at any time during the process, but can’t meet them in person.

The £100 fee also includes access to ii’s premium investor share-dealing platform, which usually costs £39.99 a month. Here, you can invest independently across the whole fund market. ii Advice’s remote advisers will only recommend funds from the myFolio range.

The funds are split into five risk levels and carry an additional 0.2pc management fee. Any other fund you pick would also carry a management fee.

The service is aimed at those with at least £100,000 in assets, according to the provider, but it will advise those with less.

The investment platform is targeting those who may not need more expensive, complicated wealth management, but would still benefit from regulated advice on investments and pensions.

However, the service has ruled out offering advice on inheritance tax, annuities, trusts, or more complex investment vehicles.

This might sound like it suits you right now, but as the number of families paying inheritance tax is predicted to double by 2031 thanks to Labour’s tax changes, increasing numbers of people will need more specialist advice.

While ii’s advisers would talk through a customer’s options around the tax, they would stop short of making a recommendation.

“We’re not trying to be all things to all people,” said Fraser Kerr, head of ii Advice.

“I would also argue that very few financial advice businesses could say that the majority of their clients are taking advantage of complex services. Actually, I’d go as far as to say that some of the more straightforward, simpler clients subsidise [more complex clients].”

Who could benefit from ii Advice?

If you require a financial adviser to recommend an investment strategy that relates broadly to retirement, investment or tax-efficient income, then ii Advice could be worth considering.

The flat £100-a-month fee could also represent good value for larger pots, compared with a standard percentage-based fee that takes an ever-greater sum as your wealth grows.

But it’s not right for everyone. Firstly, you may have more complex needs than you think. For example, a query about tax-efficient income can easily come under the remit of inheritance tax as fiscal policy changes, excluding it from ii Advice.

Say you have savings worth £150,000 and a pension worth £250,000. In previous years, inheritance tax may not have been a concern. But from April 2027, pensions will be included in an estate for tax purposes.

In this example, your pension would tip you over the £325,000 tax-free nil-rate band, exposing £75,000 to a charge of 40pc. Your ii adviser would not be able to recommend an appropriate mitigation strategy in this case.

On the other hand, if your needs are simpler, you might be able to get more advice than you think free. As of April 2026, investment companies have been able to offer regulated “targeted support”.

This is a free service that sits between guidance and fully fledged advice, and offers basic financial support based on customers in similar circumstances. For example, a retiree may be told to reduce their pension withdrawals based on the withdrawal rates of others with a similar pot and circumstances.

Some customers, meanwhile, will want personalised guidance, but won’t need ii Advice’s ongoing advice. In this case, a service such as Octopus Money’s planning service can draw up a personal financial plan for a fraction of the cost, at £299 a year.

Savings, investments and pensions would be reviewed by ii Advice, though the service would not recommend financial products or providers. But for consumers who just want to save enough to achieve their life goals, it may well be enough.

The flat fee could also be expensive for those with smaller pots. ii Advice will provide an ongoing service for a customer with a pot of £70,000, for example, despite this being lower than the £100,000 guideline.

Including the MyFolio fund charge, the annual fee would be £1,400, which equates to a percentage fee of 2pc for a £70,000 portfolio. That’s above the industry average of 1.8pc, according to NextWealth – and that fee charged by other providers would typically cover a wider spectrum of financial planning.

How does the flat fee work?

It can be difficult to understand the costs that come with financial advice, so having a flat fee can seem like an advantage. Most advice firms bundle together three separate charges for the advice, the platform that holds the investments and the cost of the fund itself. These fees are usually charged based on a percentage of a client’s assets, and so will rise with the pot.

ii Advice’s £100-a-month covers the advice and platform fee. The cost to use Aberdeen’s MyFolio fund range isn’t included, which is an annual cut of 0.2pc taken daily.

Together, these still come in at £1,400, a lower fee than the industry average of £1,800 for a £100,000 portfolio – and the ii fee stays the same regardless of portfolio size.

Percentage-based fees are common among financial advice businesses. A flat-fee approach could tempt clients, according to Heather Hopkins, the founder of research consultancy NextWealth.

Ms Hopkins said: “Clients overwhelmingly tell us they prefer fixed-fee advice. It’s simply easier to understand what you’re paying for, but only 20pc of firms offer it.”

As ii’s fee does not increase, the savings are greater for larger pots.

It is a balancing act, though. The wealthier a potential customer is, the more likely they are to require the more technical support that ii Advice doesn’t provide.

A chart on ii’s website compares this fee against traditional financial advice companies, advertising substantial savings for larger portfolios that are only being charged £100 a month.

The small print reveals the comparison is not quite like-for-like, however. The other providers – Hargreaves Lansdown, Quilter and St James’s Place – offer “a different scope of advice services”, catering to a more complete spectrum of needs.

It’s this spectrum you’ll need to consider. ii Advice represents an option for those with relatively modest pot sizes around £100,000, who want regulated advice on tax-efficient income, retail investment and retirement planning.

It could even be a very inexpensive option for wealthier customers because of its rare flat fee. But the scope for advice is more limited than the services offered by traditional financial planners, so you’ll need to weigh up whether or not it’s a false economy.

data.title: TalkTalk lenders threaten to sue over potential BT takeover
data.description:
TalkTalk’s lenders are considering legal action if BT is given approval to mount a rescue deal for the struggling broadband business.

Lenders have warned of a significant risk of lengthy legal proceedings if the former state monopoly swoops on TalkTalk. Ares Management is TalkTalk’s biggest lender.

BT has mounted an eleventh-hour attempt to take control of TalkTalk, which is scrambling to stave off a looming insolvency.

The telecoms giant has been locked in talks with government officials about how to avoid a lengthy competition review should it agree to rescue TalkTalk, which is Britain’s fourth-largest broadband provider with around 1.5 million customers.

But BT also risks opening itself up to costly and time-consuming legal action from TalkTalk’s lenders and shareholders, who are facing hundreds of millions of pounds in losses.

City sources said any litigation would depend on the nature and structure of a deal that would hand BT control of the struggling business.

It is understood that BT has had limited engagement with TalkTalk’s major creditors and shareholders, instead holding discussions directly with the Government.

Escalation of the row

The threats mark an escalation of the row that has erupted over BT’s last-minute rescue bid.

BT’s rivals, including Vodafone, Virgin Media O2, Sky and CityFibre, are expected to oppose any deal on the grounds that it would represent a major breach of competition rules.

TalkTalk’s owners, including Ares and Sir Charles Dunstone, the founder, have been seeking a buyer for the troubled business for months.

At one point, it was in negotiations to sell TalkTalk’s wholesale business, PXC, to Octopus Investments. Opus Broadband was lined up to buy the company’s consumer operations.

However, discussions with both parties broke down. Epiris, a private-equity firm, remains in talks to buy PXC, while Ares is now considered a potential suitor for the consumer business through an administration process.

As part of its offer, Epiris has asked for a three-month payment holiday from BT’s Openreach, which leases broadband lines and is TalkTalk’s biggest supplier. That waiver would be worth in the region of £200m-£250m.

However, it is understood that BT is yet to engage with Epiris over the payment holiday, which sources claimed would be required to allow the business to recover.

Should TalkTalk face administration, it would lead to significant losses for both TalkTalk’s shareholders and lenders, who have pumped hundreds of millions of pounds into the struggling business over the last few years.

US investor Ares, in particular, has stepped in to provide TalkTalk with financing over several years, including through the pandemic and the energy crisis.

Hundreds of millions could be lost

Sir Charles, who spun TalkTalk out of Carphone Warehouse in 2010, is poised to see his entire stake wiped out.

His holding was worth roughly £330m at the time of the company’s take-private deal in 2021, though it is unlikely to have been worth anything near that for some time.

TalkTalk’s latest set of accounts at the end of February 2025 showed its lowest priority bonds – which would still rank ahead of Sir Charles’s equity stake in an administration process – were trading at just 29pc of their original value.

Sir Charles also reportedly put more money into a rescue loan in 2024, which is unlikely to be recovered.

Toscafund, a British hedge fund that helped conduct the take-private deal, would also stand to lose all of its stake in the group, which was worth roughly £265m in 2021.

Ares could lose something in the region of £500m across various loans and shareholdings, with the sum potentially higher if interest is also included.

However, it is understood that in an orderly pre-pack administration, where buyers have already been lined up, Ares would expect to recover a material sum.

KKR, which provided roughly £60m in secured financing to TalkTalk, would also be in line to be repaid.

BT, TalkTalk, KKR and Ares declined to comment.

data.title: UK’s net zero strategy is an ‘abject failure’, says chemicals plant boss
data.description:
One of America’s most prominent industrialists has launched a withering attack on Britain’s “absurd” energy policy, branding the pursuit of net zero an “abject failure”.

Unable to compete with global rivals because of sky-high energy prices, UK manufacturers spanning the entire industrial base are shutting down operations or leaving altogether, billionaire Peter Huntsman warned.

Mr Huntsman, whose eponymous industrial empire includes a critical chemicals plant in Wilton, Teesside, said the charge towards renewables doesn’t make “any sense whatsoever”.

The environmental benefits of green zealotry are outweighed by “the destruction to society” caused by widespread job losses.

With energy costs “getting progressively worse”, manufacturers are asking “‘how do I get out?’ rather than ‘where can I invest?’” he added.

Yet there is an alarming “lack of urgency” from those in charge, Mr Huntsman said, with officials still intent on hitting net zero by 2050.

His criticism echoes that of Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who accused Labour of “economic vandalism on an industrial scale” after the tycoon mothballed three vital chemical plants in Hull last week.

Sir Jim blamed “ridiculously high” gas prices for the decision, claiming that UK factories are paying up to 12 times more than their rivals in the US.

This has been blamed largely on carbon taxes and the decline in domestic gas production, which has forced many factories to rely on expensive imports.

Mr Huntsman warned in March that his company could be forced to close its Wilton factory, which makes aniline, a chemical used in everything from car seats to aircraft components, if the cost of gas remained high.

The plant is the last of its kind in the country.

It is understood Huntsman is in negotiations with the Department for Business about propping up the Wilton site with funds from the Government’s £350m Critical Chemicals Resilience Fund, which was created in May to assist strategically important chemical manufacturers.

However, it is still waiting for confirmation that it qualifies for support.

“We’re still somewhat confused as to exactly what we are supposed to do to get the funds,” he said. “What are they looking for?”

Mr Huntsman said he was alarmed at suggestions that companies may have to agree to commit to using any state support for new “energy efficient” projects.

“Nobody’s putting money into new projects,” he said. “That’s just absurd.”

The Wilton plant, which employs up to 100 people, is one of the last surviving remnants of Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI), Britain’s largest manufacturer in the 20th century.

The businessman was one of the driving forces behind Huntsman’s £1.7bn takeover of what was then ICI’s industrial chemicals division in 1999.

The deal doubled Huntsman’s global workforce to 16,000 overnight and Peter became chief executive the following year, taking over from his late father Jon, who started the business in 1970 after serving in President Richard Nixon’s administration.

Within a few years, the company had shot to prominence with the invention of the “clamshell” styrofoam McDonald’s Big Mac container, and it now runs more than 55 manufacturing sites worldwide.

However, in recent years, the company’s UK operations have been bogged down energy policies that aren’t “grounded in reality”, said Mr Huntsman.

This has been compounded by the Government’s broken promises on net zero, particularly its failure to deliver a “hydrogen economy”.

“We were all told that consumers would demand carbon-free products. That never materialised,” he said.

“We were also told we were going to have cheap electricity, cheap wind power, solar power – essentially free power. Well, that didn’t work either.”

Prominent figures like himself have long warned about the dangers of allowing swathes of the steel industry and the chemicals industry to vanish.

Yet the exodus of critical manufacturers continues, he said.

“The part manufacturers that make the components for the automobile, aerospace, and pharmaceutical industries – they’re all leaving,” he said.

He added: “The question is, how bad can it get?”

Mr Huntsman said he’s not “anti-wind or anti-solar” but claimed that renewables alone couldn’t fuel an entire economy.

“Just look at energy prices,” he said. “None of this makes any sense to me whatsoever, yet I don’t see anybody seriously addressing this in government”.

He said the UK is simply “outsourcing its pollutants” by swapping domestic fossil fuel supplies for those imported from abroad, therefore “the climate is suffering too” from the Government’s net zero commitments.

As a result, Mr Huntsman said he was perplexed by Labour’s decision to ban new drilling in the North Sea while continuing to import vast quantities of oil and gas from Norway, Qatar and other overseas suppliers.

“As long as you’re buying it from somebody, you might as well buy it from yourself,” he said.

“If the UK can get to a place where it no longer uses natural gas and petrochemicals, terrific. That really would be an example to the rest of the world.

“But the simple fact of the matter is, you’re going to become more dependent on it [oil and gas] than ever before in the coming technological age.”

The UK’s preference for importing Norwegian fossil fuels over the exploitation of its own resources in the North Sea was “astounding” given that its reserves came from the same region, he said.

“Half the gas that you [Britain] consume is from Norway, and the gas that they are supplying in many parts comes from joint fields,” he said.

“They are taking hydrocarbons from underground formations that probably straddle the UK and selling it back to you.

“I don’t understand how people can look at that and say, ‘Well, it’s good that we’ve got Norway as a supplier to supply us with our own gas.’ I can’t even process that because it’s so idiotic.”

Mr Huntsman said he thought the UK’s North Sea operations were probably still doomed even if the Tories or Reform win the next election because investors won’t be willing to take the risk of Labour returning to power.

“When they do, guess who gets shut down again?” he said.

He urged the UK to take a similarly pragmatic approach to fracking and let local people decide whether it takes place in their communities.

“If they don’t want the economic benefit, that’s fine,” he said. But it should be “a national priority to try to extract it in the most economical and the most environmentally feasible way” rather than banning it on safety grounds.

“Usually in society – particularly in the UK – when something was declared unsafe, you didn’t abandon it,” he said. “You just made it better.

“The first steam engines that were ever built were blowing up all the time. The first railroads were terribly unsafe, but we got better and in the United States we have made fracking work.”

As for the threat from cheap Chinese imports, he urged Britain to follow America’s path by getting tougher on trade.

“Does that mean going to war with China? Of course it doesn’t. But it does mean choosing the industries that you’re going to protect, just like the Chinese protect certain industries in their country, and just like we do in the US,” he said.

He also warned against partnering with the Chinese in the way that Nissan is proposing doing with Chery at its Sunderland plant: “I would say be very careful. The Chinese are going to import batteries, motors, frames.

“They’ll say the car’s made in the UK. It might be glued together [in the UK], but that’s not a car built in the UK. You’re not getting the economic benefit.”

In June, Huntsman unveiled a blockbuster all-stock merger with American rival Olin to create a new chemicals giant with $12.5bn (£9.5bn) of combined annual turnover.

However, with energy prices still elevated in Britain, Mr Huntsman admitted that the future of the company’s Wilton site remained uncertain.

There was a moment during the summer when a fall in energy prices meant it was breaking even, but he warned that the site was now back to losing money.

He says its future rests on two things: firstly, whether the energy shocks of the last few years are “event-driven” or “systemic”; and secondly, “How long can you withstand the tides with a government that just doesn’t seem to care?”

Mr Huntsman will be watching closely to see how the Government responds to Ineos’s decision to mothball three plants in Hull.

“I’ve read that Jim Ratcliffe is playing chicken with the Government,” he said. “That’s a hell of a game of chicken.

“As soon as you shut down a plant, three things happen: you start losing employees, you’re putting strain on your operations, and you’re losing your customers. It’s not a question of just flipping the switch back on again.”

data.title: Poundland bosses in battle with owner over retailer’s future
data.description:
Bosses at Poundland have appointed advisers to spearhead a possible management buyout in a challenge to the chain’s owners.

Management has drafted in consultants from Interpath to work on a potential bid as part of an increasingly fraught battle with Poundland’s owners over the company’s future.

Gordon Brothers plunged the business into turmoil by unexpectedly putting it up for sale in August. The move raised fears that Poundland could be tipped into administration, prompting insurers to stop offering new cover to suppliers.

Alvarez and Marsal has been hired by Gordon Brothers to oversee the sale process. Interpath’s appointment highlights a growing split between management and Poundland’s owners.

Barry Williams, the managing director, has partnered with Andy Bond, the former Asda boss, to lead a proposed management buyout, with an offer submitted to Gordon Brothers earlier this week.

Their bid does not propose any store closures and is believed to be fully financed by an unnamed UK backer.

It is thought that the offer is unlikely to meet the £30m price tag Gordon Brothers has put on Poundland, a business it acquired for just £1 last summer.

However, industry sources said it had the support of Pepco, Poundland’s former owner, which still holds a 30pc stake in the retailer.

The offer from management rivals separate bids from other suitors, which could include Poundstretcher owner Fortress Investment Group and Modella Capital, which owns TG Jones.

Some rival retailers are understood to be hoping to cherry-pick Poundland’s best stores – a move that would lead to the company being broken up. Poundland employs 11,000 people across 600 stores.

Insurers halt vital cover

The Telegraph revealed last week that management had been scrambling to reassure suppliers after Gordon Brothers announced a quickfire sale process last month.

Alvarez and Marsal’s appointment fuelled suspicion that Gordon Brothers was planning to put the company into administration and make a quick profit by offloading whatever remained of its stock.

Though Gordon Brothers primarily invests in highly distressed companies, it also owns a liquidation business that made money from closing about 200 Poundland stores last year.

Uncertainty over the retailer’s future has led to insurers no longer offering new cover to suppliers of Poundland. One insurer has also withdrawn cover altogether.

Poundland made pre-tax losses of £85m in the 12 months ending Sept 2025. Accounts revealed a cash pile of more than £30m and several sources of borrowing.

In trading figures released last week, management said performance at Poundland was improving.

A spokesman said: “Profitability is on a strongly improving trajectory with expected pre-tax earnings around £80m better than last year.”

Shaun Wills, the finance chief, said: “The fundamentals of this business are strong.”

Poundland and Gordon Brothers were contacted for comment.

data.title: NatWest in new debanking row with shipping tycoon
data.description:
NatWest has become embroiled in a fresh debanking row after a US tycoon accused the lender of closing his account on false grounds.

Philip Adkins, an international shipping executive, claims NatWest’s private bank Coutts removed him as a customer based on inaccurate information it held about his finances.

Mr Adkins’s lawyers have claimed that Coutts incorrectly put his wealth at £62m, said he owned an apartment in Hong Kong and said he had lost half his wealth in a credit line to Goldman Sachs.

Instead, he had never owned an apartment nor had a relationship with Goldman Sachs, his lawyers said, adding that he had been a Coutts customer for four decades. His lawyers also claimed his net worth figure was incorrect.

The case echoes the debanking scandal involving Nigel Farage, whose account Coutts closed in 2023.

The incident led to the exit of Dame Alison Rose, the bank’s chief executive, who admitted discussing Mr Farage’s case with a BBC journalist.

Mr Adkins has launched a data-protection claim alleging that Coutts’s inaccurate information triggered an investigation into his finances in the US and led to his daughter’s detention.

The former chief executive of shipping group Red Box Energy Services alleges that “false” Coutts records caused him “serious distress”.

He is seeking compensation from Coutts, legal costs and other expenses, an order requiring the bank to delete or rectify the records and a declaration that it breached data protection laws.

Coutts is defending the claim, which it called “speculative” in legal filings, according to the Financial Times, which first reported the case.

The lender added that the UK and US authorities sanctioned entities connected to Red Box Energy Services in 2024.

It denies sharing any data with US prosecutors, claiming Mr Adkins supplied the information himself and requested to close his accounts with Coutts.

The private bank also said that it must comply with anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations.

Coutts is one of Britain’s most esteemed banks, known as the “Queen’s bank” for its lengthy relationship with Elizabeth II.

During the Farage incident, NatWest initially claimed the Reform leader had failed to meet eligibility requirements for access to the bank, but it was subsequently revealed that the closure was because of his political views.

A report by the law firm Travers Smith found that although NatWest had acted within the law, it had made “serious failings” in the incident.

Dame Alison later admitted a “serious error of judgment” after briefing a BBC journalist about Mr Farage’s case, which forced her resignation from the bank.

Last year, the bank paid Mr Farage an undisclosed sum to settle the dispute.

NatWest declined to comment on Mr Adkins’ case.

Mr Adkins said: “The UK GDPR sets clear standards for UK financial institutions when processing personal data, particularly in relation to accuracy. I am confident that the court will ensure those standards are properly upheld.”

data.title: The risky private funds targeting pensioners
data.description:
When Labour started ramping up its inheritance tax (IHT) assault after it came to power, it’s unlikely party apparatchiks had any inkling it would inadvertently fuel a little-known industry of giant private-market funds.

Originally intended as a relief for family-owned businesses, schemes seeking to help people avoid IHT have quietly mushroomed into one of the UK’s most-exploited tax loopholes with billions of pounds invested.

Under the rules, HMRC allows all of an investment’s value to pass to your heirs entirely free of IHT as long as you invest in a qualifying business for at least two years before you die.

It’s a loophole that a number of enterprising financiers have since realised can be used as a platform for investment funds.

It works like this: funds are constructed of hundreds of unlisted businesses, each of which qualifies for “business relief” – the name of the loophole – and are then marketed as a convenient way to avoid inheritance tax.

These schemes have hit the headlines in recent weeks after the problems at Octopus Inheritance Tax Service (OITS), the biggest of these funds and poster child for the sector.

OITS raised billions from 18,000 pensioners with the promise of lowering their IHT bills.

However, they have been trapped in the scheme since July after Octopus blocked withdrawals as it finalised a takeover which risked changing the value of their investments.

It has proved a warning shot for the industry.

But beyond OITS, the sector is booming and tens of thousands of pensioners have invested approximately £10bn in six of the largest schemes, which have then funnelled that money into all sorts of assets that meet the bare conditions for business relief.

This has raised questions over whether the loophole is being readily exploited – and what Labour can do to fix it.

As a rule, the assets in these schemes must be privately held in order to qualify for business relief.

They can often be collections of hundreds of different unlisted businesses, making them difficult to value and meaning shareholders can often risk being left in the dark.

Even the City watchdog has concerns.

“Business relief investments are complex, higher-risk products that won’t be suitable for everyone,” the Financial Conduct Authority says.

For opponents, however, a bigger sin is that several of the funds invest in assets that have little bearing on the UK economy.

Arun Advani, an economics professor from the University of Warwick, says that few of the funds in this sector are likely to be the sort of high-growth businesses that might support the UK economy.

“[The relief] encourages fund managers to look for things that are going to be as non-volatile as possible. Nobody’s investing in this because they actually think their assets are going to increase hugely in value,” he says.

One example is Downing, a London-based fund manager which caters to almost 8,000 investors. Its energy fund has a substantial portfolio of Nordic renewable products (Downing says it pays British tax on the profits generated by all of the assets, including the Nordic portion) far from UK shores.

Foresight Group, another scheme, makes the vast majority of its investments in the UK but has also funnelled investors’ money into land-based trout farms in Norway.

Another, Triple Point, uses its tax breaks to acquire frontline ambulances and essential medical equipment, then wins contracts from the NHS to lease the products back to them.

“Why is this the thing we’re giving a tax break to?” Advani says of the IHT schemes.

Another criticism is the fees charged to pensioners.

Across five years, savers can expect to pay anywhere between £13.55 and £18.47 per £100 invested, depending on the scheme – a sizeable chunk of cash if the investments run into the tens of thousands of pounds.

According to Tax Efficient Review, one of the highest fees is charged by Puma Heritage, another major supplier that makes loans to the care home and the student accommodation sector.

It charges roughly eight different fees which are ultimately paid by its investors.

A number of Puma’s fees are tied to the overall performance of the fund. These include a 0.4pc fee derived from the net asset value of the fund and an annual “advisory fee” that is only charged if it consistently hits its performance target of 3pc returns a year.

Except in its first year, Puma Heritage has returned between 3.1pc and 3.6pc every year.

Puma has also boasted of “0pc capital losses to date” on more than £2bn lent since it launched in 2013.

However, it lent to two developments linked to a care home developer in 2019 and both entered liquidation in 2023 after none of the apartments sold, leaving Puma facing a shortfall of around £1.8m, according to the company’s liquidators.

Sources close to the company claim the shortfall was related to accrued interest and fees rather than the capital.

Puma took control of the underlying developments that year and has attempted to sell the apartments to recover the loans. So far, it has been unable to recover the vast majority of the loan balance but has yet to record it as a capital loss.

Part of the reason these complex IHT schemes have boomed in popularity is because of Labour’s moves to curb which investments qualify for IHT.

Since taking power, the Government has made the IHT relief for shares listed on the junior stock market, the Alternative Investment Market (AIM), comparatively less generous and subjected unused pensions to IHT as well.

One major provider of AIM IHT solutions, which declined to be named, says it saw roughly £500,000 leave to Downing’s schemes over the course of a week.

Another, Whitman Asset Management, estimates that £1bn has flowed into private business relief schemes out of the AIM market.

Schemes are also using increasingly sophisticated measures to allow potential investors to efficiently avoid IHT.

Despite these funds taking in new money all the time, they also allow pensioners to buy new shares which can also lower tax bills.

Because of the quirks in the tax code, if an investor already has money in a fund, any more invested through a rights issue automatically becomes IHT-free without the two-year wait.

It means investors can keep ploughing money into the scheme and avoiding IHT.

With the implicit backing of the Treasury and Labour, these schemes are set to grow both in number and in size.

“[These schemes] are extremely complicated,” says Nouran Moustafa, the founder of Roxton Wealth, a financial advice firm that does not recommend business relief schemes.

“I don’t really think anyone would understand that scheme’s ins and outs unless you’re the one who created the scheme.”
