data.title: Barclays backs down as WFH workers revolt
data.description:
Barclays has backed down over its return-to-the-office plans after facing a revolt by thousands of staff.

The bank has delayed an overhaul of its hybrid-working policy that would have forced employees to work from the office three days a week.

The policy was meant to come into force on Monday, but staff have been told it will now only be introduced at the start of 2027, after a transition period.

Until then, staff will be encouraged to comply but will not be required to.

“We are extending the implementation period for UK colleagues to ensure colleagues have the right support as we move through the transition,” staff were told in a memo, according to the Financial Times.

“You will not be required to meet the new arrangements until the start of 2027,” the memo from the executive committee of Barclays continued.

The compromise comes after staff rebelled over demands to come in more often. Employees demanded extra pay to cover commuting costs and called for exemptions for any employees whose commutes were longer than 40 minutes.

Thousands of Barclays employees signed an open letter coordinated by Unite, which represents 80pc of the lender’s 45,000 staff.

Barclays’ push to get staff back to the office is in line with wider efforts by City firms to reverse remote-working policies that were introduced during the Covid-19 pandemic.

White-collar workers at some of the world’s biggest companies have resisted the change.

In an extreme case, TSB staff have started preparing legal action over plans to force them to work in the office three days a week following the takeover by Santander.

The Government has vowed to make it harder for employers to block staff from working remotely, with plans to force businesses to “properly consider” flexible work requests. The changes would require companies to offer a face-to-face meeting with staff to explain why their homeworking requests had been rejected.

A Barclays spokesman said: “Our updated onsite working arrangements will take effect as planned. We have continued to listen to colleague feedback to ensure colleagues have the right support while enabling us to deliver the benefits of working together in person.

“This includes transitional measures for those whose personal circumstances currently prevent them from meeting the new arrangements.”

data.title: Dyson increases payout to £750m despite tariff hit
data.description:
Dyson has paid out £750m to its billionaire founder’s holding company despite the engineering giant recording a fall in profits from Donald Trump’s tariffs.

Accounts for Weybourne Holdings, the Singapore-based parent company owned by the Dyson family, revealed a significant increase in dividends last year.

Sir James Dyson’s business paid out £750m in 2025, up from £200m the previous year and the most generous payout since 2022.

It came despite the company facing a sales hit from tariffs and weak consumer confidence.

Dyson revealed in March that sales fell from £6.57bn to £6.13bn last year. Accounts published in Singapore this week also revealed that pre-tax profits had dropped from £561m to £511m.

It said that sales had taken a £440m hit from US tariffs, but that operating profits had grown in spite of the hit.

Dyson cut hundreds of jobs last year, including around a third of its employees in the UK.

Weybourne, which is owned by the Dyson family and manages investments including Sir James’s farming initiatives and various investments. It owns 100pc of Dyson, best known for its vacuum cleaners and hair dryers.

Dyson has cut its payouts to Weybourne in recent years, from a record £1.2bn in 2022 to £700m and then £200m in 2023 and 2024 respectively.

A spokesman said: “The new US tariffs were a very substantial cost to Dyson in 2025. Without them, our 2025 profits before tax would have been higher than 2024.

“Even so, our Ebitda (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) grew 18pc and our operating profit 15pc, which reflects a strong year with the most ever products launched.”

This year, Dyson been facing teething issues over the launch of its £420 CameraJet toothbrush, with the company saying some models were malfunctioning due to water leaks, resulting in the device going out of stock.

It says the production problems have since been resolved.

Sir James is Britain’s 13th-richest person, according to the Sunday Times rich list, with a net worth of £12bn.

Dyson moved its registered corporate headquarters from Britain to Singapore in 2019 with Sir James moving his residency back to Britain in 2021.

His farming group is one of Britain’s biggest by land ownership and has invested hundreds of millions in new technology.

The majority of Dyson’s production takes place in south-east Asia including Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.

data.title: Diesel car values crash as pump prices reach record high
data.description:
The price of second-hand diesel cars is falling sharply as the fuel hits a new high at the pumps.

Used diesel vehicles were advertised at an average of £13,802 last month, according to Autotrader. That was £850 lower than at the start of the US war with Tehran and just £400 higher than in September 2016.

By comparison, Autotrader figures showed the average asking price for a used diesel peaked at almost £18,000 in January 2022, up 25pc in less than a year.

The drop in recent months comes as diesel prices reach new highs in the UK. Donald Trump’s threat to ring-fence diesel supplies for American drivers has seen pump prices climb to a record £2 a litre during the weekend, with analysts suggesting it could hit £2.50 or even £3 if the Iran war drags on.

Second-hand diesels rode a price boom in the years leading to 2022, amid moves by successive governments to take internal-combustion-engine cars off British roads. That culminated in the Zero Emission Vehicle mandate that will outlaw their sale from 2030.

Diesel car production has consequently dropped 60pc in a decade, increasing the scarcity value of the cars and funnelling buyers into the second-hand market.

Some motorists favour diesel because of engine efficiency, and the latest models comply with tighter emissions standards. Diesel cars deliver anywhere between 12pc and 19pc more miles to the gallon than petrol equivalents.

However, valuations have dropped in recent years as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the outbreak of the Iran conflict have pushed up oil prices and the fuels derived from it.

Prices for used petrol vehicles have also declined, though by much less, reflecting higher fuel supply from refineries. Diesel is priced at around 14pc more than petrol across UK forecourts.

Philip Gomm at the RAC Foundation said: “Thousands of people who are in the market for a second-hand diesel car will be doing back-of-the-envelope calculations to decide whether it’s time to change fuel type.

“Drivers are acutely aware of pump prices because it’s the only product we buy on a daily basis where the cost is displayed in front of us to a tenth of a penny.”

The cost of a tank of diesel may be nearing the point where the greater efficiency of diesel cars compared with petrol models was outweighed by the cost of the fuel, Mr Gomm said.

The improving availability of cheap electric vehicles may also hasten the retreat of diesel.

The RAC Foundation said that while private motorists could change fuel types, that was not the case for the owners of Britain’s fleet of 4.8 million diesel vans.

Mr Gomm said: “For the small businesses that rely on these vehicles, there aren’t practical alternatives. They are hostage to high diesel prices and so are their customers.”

data.title: Chinese imports ‘threaten to wipe out UK industries in five years’
data.description:
Cut-price Chinese manufacturers could wipe out whole chunks of British industry within five years, a think tank has warned.

Chatham House said European and UK industries ranging from electric vehicles and machine tools, to wind turbines and pharmaceuticals were “on a trajectory to lose” to China’s fast-growing and technologically dominant companies.

“There is a real possibility that over the next five years, Europe will lose much of its industrial base to Chinese competition,” said James Kynge, a Chatham House fellow and author of a new report on the economic threat from China.

“Not only will this result in the further loss of jobs and expertise; it may also mean the loss of companies with long histories of technological excellence and contributions to local communities.”

Mr Kynge said Chinese companies were winning because the country’s huge domestic market gave them greater economies of scale. China also boasted world-class universities, cutting-edge technological innovation and generous state subsidies.

He warned that British companies were losing market share to Chinese rivals not only at home in the UK, but also in China and in other countries where they competed.

“Chinese competitors are going global and rising to the forefront of global technology. That means that a UK business anywhere in the world is going to experience blowback from these uber-competitors coming out of China,” he said.

The soaring cost of energy is hindering British industry’s ability to compete and last week Britain’s biggest pharmaceutical companies warned of “a slow agony of decline” in the face of China’s growing dominance.

The Chatham House report found that in the pharmaceutical sector, China could rip through the clinical development of new drugs at three times the pace of Europe, for half the cost.

Mr Kynge said British and European pharmaceutical firms were now getting Chinese players to develop drugs for them. “They are outsourcing their brains to China. The collateral damage will be an atrophication of the UK’s own ability to innovate in drugs in the future,” he said.

The report also looked at China’s increasing takeover of industries such as wind turbines, machine tools and cars, where Europe until recently still held the upper hand.

The EU is reportedly about to launch new measures to protect its industries from cut-price Chinese imports. But Britain has remained more open to Chinese trade.

‘We need to do a reverse-China on China’

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, told The Telegraph this month that “if you put trade protections up, you’ve got to understand that they’ll probably be reciprocated and you’ll lose out”.

Britain had a £52.5bn deficit in its goods trade with China in the 12 months to the end of March. Goods exports to China declined 0.5pc to £18.5bn, while imports rose 2.4pc to £71bn.

Mr Kynge said the Government needed to reduce the regulatory burden and speed up bureaucratic processes to help British companies compete. Britain also needed to build more infrastructure, and increase the tech skills of its workforce.

Britain should welcome Chinese investment in non-sensitive sectors, he added, as long as the investors transferred technology, used local suppliers or hired and trained British workers.

“These were the conditions of entry for many of the European companies that went to China in the early days – you had to transfer technology. So we need to do a reverse-China on China,” he said.

data.title: Councils handed power to seize empty homes after just six months
data.description:
Labour has been accused of threatening property rights after giving councils the power to seize empty homes after six months.

Ministers are cutting the period a property must be vacant before local authorities can take control from two years to six months.

The property will remain privately owned, but councils can take control through an Empty Dwelling Management Order, which allows them to take over its management and rent it out for up to seven years.

Councils will also no longer have to provide evidence of problems such as anti-social behaviour before seeking to take control, as they do currently.

Labour is also exploring further changes to make officials more likely to use the powers, including measures to protect local authorities from the costs of taking over empty properties.

Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, said bringing empty homes back into use “can help solve the housing crisis”.

However, the changes triggered a backlash from Conservative politicians and property campaigners, who accused Labour of eroding property rights.

Writing on X, Kevin Hollinrake, a former Conservative minister, said: “The Loony Left are always keen to revoke our fundamental rights when it becomes convenient to do so; on this occasion, property rights.

“Seizing someone’s home because you disapprove of how they use it is classic socialist authoritarianism.”

Lord Frost, the former Brexit minister, said: “Don’t risk leaving your house empty. After six months the Government will come for it and rent it to someone else.”

Labour argues the new powers target homes left unused for long periods, rather than properties temporarily vacant between owners or during legitimate works.

Emily Thornberry, a Labour MP, said: “I said it in 2020, and I’ll say it again. If you leave a home empty long-term in the middle of a housing crisis, it should be seized. Today’s announcement is great news.”

More than 300,000 homes in England were classed as long-term empty last year, according to official figures.

There were 303,185 properties vacant for at least six months in October 2025, up 14.5pc from 264,884 a year earlier. Long-term empty homes accounted for 1.2pc of England’s housing stock.

That figure includes properties left vacant for a range of reasons, including homes awaiting probate, undergoing renovation or being prepared for sale.

Ministers said the changes would allow councils to stop property from falling into serious disrepair while helping provide homes for families in need. This could reduce the need to carry out renovations after taking over management of the property.

However, Kirstie Allsopp, a television presenter and property commentator, questioned whether councils had the capacity to make use of the new powers.

She said: “Most councils can’t grant planning permission for a downstairs loo without six months’ notice; the idea that they’ll be seizing properties and renovating them is an absolute fantasy.”

The Government says no applications for an order have been made since 2021.

Councils have been able to seek orders to take over the management of empty homes since 2006, when the threshold was six months. A two-year threshold was introduced in 2012.

data.title: Housebuilders get £2bn bounce from Burnham’s new Help to Buy scheme
data.description:
Housebuilders’ valuations have surged by £2bn after Andy Burnham unveiled a new home loan scheme for first-time buyers.

Shares in Britain’s biggest listed builders soared on Monday morning on hopes that the new scheme, called Your First Home, would ignite a wave of demand and drive up woeful building rates.

Barratt Redrow, Bellway Homes, MJ Gleeson and Persimmon Homes were all up by between 12pc and 18pc as of 12pm, while Bloomberg’s FTSE 350 subindex for the sector surged by as much as 16pc – a record rise.

The collective value of the UK’s eight largest builders rose by £2bn, according to analysis by RBC Capital Markets.

The Your First Home scheme, set to be introduced in next month’s Budget, will allow first-time buyers to purchase new-build properties with a 2.5pc deposit and a 20pc government-backed equity loan scheme with an initial interest-free period.

Buyers will only be able to access the scheme if their income is below a certain threshold and the property they are buying is below a local price cap.

Analysts said the scheme could bring tens of thousands of additional new-build homes each year.

The scheme is a revised version of the Help to Buy equity loan scheme that was introduced by George Osborne, the Conservative chancellor, in 2013 and ran for a decade.

However, Mr Burnham’s iteration allows first-time buyers to purchase with a smaller 2.5pc deposit, rather than 5pc under Help to Buy, and will include an as-yet-unspecified contribution from developers.

The scheme will be a lifeline for housebuilders grappling with a toxic cocktail of materials cost inflation, new regulations and low buyer demand that has been heavily constrained by high mortgage rates.

Analysts have previously warned that Labour is on track to miss its central manifesto promise to build 1.5 million homes over this parliament by more than half after planning consents slumped to their lowest in more than 20 years last year.

Barratt Redrow, Britain’s biggest housebuilder, was down by around a fifth this year until Monday.

Anthony Codling, an RBC analyst, said: “Your First Home has the potential to be a huge stimulus for housing supply. If it follows the footsteps of Help to Buy, it could potentially be responsible for around half of the new homes built.”

The introduction of the previous Help to Buy scheme in 2013 triggered a 31pc increase in housing starts in its first year.

Marcus Dixon, the head of residential research at JLL consultants, said: “If we see a 31pc increase to annual starts in England, it could mean an additional 40,000, which would get us to 170,000.”

Mr Codling said housebuilders such as Crest Nicholson with greater exposure to the south of England, where buyer demand is most constrained by affordability, will see the biggest boost from the scheme.

Those such as Berkeley Homes which focus on higher-priced homes that are likely to exceed the caps will see the least difference, he said.

Building materials suppliers also soared, with concrete manufacturer Forterra jumping by 15pc and brick maker Ibstock up 21pc.

However, Aynsley Lammin, an analyst at Investec, warned it was vital that the scheme be implemented in time for the 2027 spring selling season, otherwise it could bring a further fall in transactions.

He said: “There is a question about when and how quickly the scheme will be implemented and there is a risk that a significant delay could cause nearer-term first-time buyer purchases to be deferred.”

data.title: I travelled the ‘border’ between North and South. Here’s what I learnt
data.description:
A sign by the estuary warns of danger, but it’s hard to see much to be afraid of here apart from the nettles and a fairly ominous sky. Under the Severn Bridge, on a spit of land on the river’s west side, it seems peaceful enough. Traffic roars overhead, but you can’t see the cars from below. There’s birdsong and the smell of wet foliage, glimmering water fringed by sodden sand and then cracked earth. It doesn’t feel like a border, but I’m standing at the far western end of England’s North-South divide.

There is, of course, no official line across England’s midriff. No razor-wire fences or passport checks mark where the South ends and the North begins. But nor is the boundary a figment of our imagination. We’ve heard enough jokes about the Watford Gap to know that Southerners see the North – the people, the places, the culture – as somehow different. And we Northerners, admittedly, can be bloody-minded about our Northern identity.

But how entrenched does the North-South divide remain today, after years of political talk of levelling up, Northern powerhouses and ill-fated high-speed rail connections? How much does our geography still shape how we see those from elsewhere in the country? And where, actually, does the notional dividing line start and end?

Apparently, not where you might expect. Recent YouGov data from almost 46,000 adults in England revealed that many people along the borders of the areas classified as North, South and Midlands don’t place themselves in the same regions government maps would suggest. Feelings of “Northernness” extended south of the regional borders, the pollsters found, while in the parts of East Anglia that supposedly sit in the South, people don’t all feel Southern. In short, like many types of identity, it’s complicated.

With that in mind, I have set out to travel along an unofficial boundary line between the North and South of England – one commonly used in academic research – to interrogate these feelings and explore what the divide means today. My editor has suggested I walk the entire 340 miles from Beachley Point on the Severn estuary to the Wash, between Lincolnshire and Norfolk, possibly in one go. I have counter-suggested the use of a motor vehicle.

The journey is a personal one. Having grown up in Leeds, my Northern identity is one I have insisted on throughout my adult life (which I’ve spent mostly in the South). When I started writing my debut crime thriller novel, The House on Otley Road, I knew it had to be set in West Yorkshire. Home.

The tug of the North has never left me, and I spend much of my time on the East Coast Main Line, travelling to and from where I spent my youth. But I’m surprised to find that it supposedly begins more or less where I’m standing by the Severn. The first (and only) person I encounter on the footpath here is Justin Charnock, 37. He identifies as Southern (this is fair – he comes from near Bristol) and thinks “people in the North are a lot nicer than people in the South” (also fair). “More welcoming,” he says.

It’s a commonly held perception, mentioned frequently by those I meet on my journey – almost all of whom have strong ideas about how Northerners differ from Southerners.

Charnock thinks being Southern traditionally means being “wealthier; a lot more aloof; snobby; much less hospitable, welcoming, friendly or helpful”. Working in the South West (he won’t divulge his job), he never gets tipped and “often people are a bit snooty”.

‘It’s become very middle class here’

Behind the popular images of Northerners lie some dispiriting numbers. The North East remains the region with the lowest healthy life expectancy at birth (HLE), at 57 years, according to the most recent figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS). It has had the lowest HLE in every period since the ONS began measuring it. The South East remains the region with the highest HLE (63 years for men, 64.3 years for women).

A similar disparity can be seen in economic activity. In 2023, London had the highest gross domestic product per capita, at £69,077, while the North East had the lowest, at £28,583. It is worth noting, though, that the poverty rate is higher in London (26 per cent) than anywhere else in the country, according to figures from the charity Joseph Rowntree Foundation.

Meanwhile, perceptions of Northerners and Southerners that seem to stem from our economic histories – the North as industrial, the South as the country’s financial engine – have stubbornly persisted.

The first stop on my journey is Brockweir, a scenic Gloucestershire village on the river Wye. Old stone houses are painted in creamy yellow, pale blue and white, while green hills rise behind them. All the villagers seem to know each other. They all have dogs, and their dogs know each other too. The community owns its pub, the 16th-century Brockweir Inn.

“We tried to sell our bodies [to raise the money for it], but we’re all too old,” says Carol Knight, 76. (I think she’s joking.)

Her family has lived here for centuries. “It’s become very middle class,” says the suntanned, denim-dungaree-clad former English teacher, while clutching a bunch of Whitsuntide boss flowers and the leads of her two labradors. “Property prices have skyrocketed.”

Does this mean Brockweir must be Southern? House prices are, after all, a stark divider between North and South. Prices may be rising more steeply in the North at present, but the gap remains vast, even after removing London from the equation: in March 2026, the average house price across the South East and South West was £340,000, compared with £188,500 across the North East and North West.

‘We need more Northern leaders’

I travel onwards, trying to keep close to the Wye, down winding lanes bordered by verdant hedgerows and cow parsley. I stop at Upper Redbrook, where I can’t find a pub, or a shop, or a human, then Staunton, where the 18th-century pub isn’t open yet (it’s still too early). Traffic rattles through the village of silent modern houses.

In the Herefordshire village of Lea, I encounter a friendly pair of Scousers who decamped here long ago. Mike Tyson, a 46-year-old roofer and carpenter (“Yes, it’s my real name,” he says, for probably the millionth time), talks of his daughter’s “Northern attitude”.

What is it? “Friendlier, more easy-come, easy-go. ‘Chippy’ is the right phrase.”

The men are not the only ones to claim Northerners have a different (better?) sense of humour. But there’s uncertainty about whether we’re in the North or the South here – the consensus seems to be the middle – but Tyson believes there’s more money to be made down here than up in Liverpool.

Tied up with the question of economic activity and affluence is that of political power. Devolution to England’s cities and regions has given some control to communities far from Westminster. Whether it has helped those communities feel less overlooked is uncertain. Phil Henesey, 71, who is drinking in a beer garden with Tyson in the late-afternoon sunshine, says the North still feels farther (figuratively) from Westminster decision making.

“That’s why we need more Northern leaders,” he says.

He is speaking not long before the enthroning of a Northern leader in Downing Street. Andy Burnham, the Liverpool-born former Mayor of Greater Manchester, has made much of his links to, and concern for, the North of England. The new PM has created a No 10 North. In doing so, he has set himself up to be judged on how successfully he makes Northerners feel more connected to the centre of power. Also on how he does this without alienating the South.

‘There’s more chivalry in the North’

It’s raining when I reach Ledbury, the sky a grey-white sheet. The Tudor buildings are picture-perfect and well preserved. “It’s very much Middle England,” says a shopkeeper on the high street who doesn’t want to be named. “Did you ever see Keeping up Appearances? It’s full of Hyacinth Buckets [here].”

He identifies as a Southerner. “When you go up North, it’s dark,” he says. “It’s a funny old thing, that divide.”

Declan Butler, a 68-year-old Irishman who moved to Britain in the 1970s and now runs a gift shop down the road, thinks Ledbury is “probably more Southern”, judging by its disposable income.

“I had a couple in here from North Yorkshire at the weekend and they spoke to me as if we were old friends, whereas people from the South East are much more reserved,” he says. “If I was to choose a Southerner or a Northerner to be friends with, I’d choose a Northerner, because they’re friendlier. They’re probably harder workers. They’re grafters.”

He concedes that Cockneys and people from Essex can be friendly, too. Has he been to the North much? “I’ve been to Birmingham,” he offers.

Crossing into Worcestershire, I see the grey-blue shadow of the hills rise up ahead. I pass an old roadside chapel and an abandoned filling station, and arrive at Bredon, where the local Spar sells cider on tap.

“I thought the North started at Crewe,” muses Steve Fowler, an ex-Army man, inside the still-quiet Royal Oak pub, where there’s horse racing on the TV. He’s surprised to hear that by some definitions he is in the North right now. A Southerner by birth (Surrey), he awards the North another point for humour. “The funniest comedians are Northerners,” he says.

“I think [people] are more materialistic in the South,” says David Gray, a semi-retired gardener from Scotland. “There’s a lot more chivalry in the North.”

“It’s all about survival in the North,” chips in Paul Sefton, a retired butcher. He came here from North Wales 30 years ago “purely because someone said to me my kids would never get a proper job up North”.

‘The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties’

The North-South divide has been with us for a long time, chronicled and perpetuated by our art and culture. Elizabeth Gaskell’s North and South (published 1855) contrasts England’s tranquil, idyllic South with a grimy industrial North plagued by poverty and suffering. Almost 150 years later, David Peace evoked a dark and lawless North in his fictional Red Riding quartet. There was always something harder and edgier about the most famous Northern bands than their Southern counterparts. Contrast the Beatles with the Kinks, Oasis with Blur.

Yet in today’s hyperconnected society, how long can such differences last?

“It’s flattened out quite a bit by sheer mobility,” says Steve Fowler. And, he says, by exposure to the internet. “You would have to go very deep into the countryside, to very isolated communities, to find residual differences.”

In the Plough Inn in Stretton-on-Fosse, Warwickshire, Gordon Everett, 59, says, with both sadness and pride, “This is one of the last old-fashioned drinking pubs.” Local accents are waning a lot, he says, touching on the most overt marker of Northern or Southern identity. When he was a boy, you could tell the difference in accents between people from two local villages that lay just three miles apart. “Now, everyone’s got this flat English accent.”

Non-locals, he says, have come to the area and changed it. “The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties.”

Still, tracing this line across the country is a lesson in the extent to which our villages and small towns either cling to their past or else are haunted by it. Between Bredon and Stretton-on-Fosse, I pass houses with names such as the Old Bakehouse, the Old Stoves. A croquet club and a country clothing store. Less picturesque: a dead badger on the A44.

In Brackley, Northamptonshire, there’s a similar nostalgia in evidence. On the high street, there’s the Old Bakery and the Old Hall Bookshop. The sign for Brackley Community Shops is painted in old-fashioned fairground colours. One of these shops offers tattoos, but still.

In the Courtyard Shops farther along, I’m reminded of one of those mock-Victorian streets you find in museums, except there’s a vape shop here. Browsers are welcome, says a sticker in the window, and they’re also on CCTV.

A 75-year-old woman I meet in the town, when I ask what Northerners are like, suggests they’re either industrious farmers or else they work in “industrial places”. I don’t have the heart to tell her that no one I know in West Yorkshire does any such thing.

Did you know Brackley is in fact north of the North-South divide, I ask Anne Mellor, a volunteer in a local charity shop? “No,” she says, “we thought we were in the middle, surrounded by HS2.”

Depending on where you are in the North, transport links can be a sore point – and another marker of difference from the South. Burnham might be proud of his re-regulated Bee Network buses in Manchester, but raise the subject of the still-non-existent tram service in Leeds and that fabled Northern grit might give way to heavy sighs of Northern frustration.

In the North East, poor transport links were said last year to put more than 30 per cent of the region at risk of poverty. In 2022, lack of transport connectivity was found by the Centre for Cities to cost the North £16bn a year in productivity losses. Against this backdrop, HS2 has become a punchline, not an answer.

‘They’re parochial and territorial’

I’m travelling to Silverstone, Northamptonshire, which is famous for a different sort of transport. Pictures of motor-racing heroes adorn the walls of the village pub, the White Horse. I pass through a familiar landscape of roundabouts and roadworks before arriving. A poster on the village noticeboard invites me to become the best version of myself. (I decline.)

Gary Baird, 38, who runs the pub, thinks the North is more working class, while the South attracts more tourism. No one, he argues, goes to Hull on holiday.

Onwards to Rushden, Northants, a “historic boot and shoe town”, passing en route an American diner, a Starbucks, a Travelodge, a McDonald’s, a Toby Carvery and a new-build housing estate. I could be anywhere now. I don’t know whether I’m North or South, my senses are scrambled, or numbed by the dreary uniformity of our in-between spaces.

But in Rushden, for the first time, I feel I could be in the North. Behind the bar in the town’s Working Men’s Club, 30-year-old Tomethia Bartley confirms, “They’re Northerners here.” (She’s not – she’s from London.) “They’re all in a community together. Everyone knows everyone.”

She’s wearing a T-shirt saying, “Don’t like me? F--- off. Problem solved.” I don’t know how Northern or Southern this sentiment is.

Howard, 67, a former helicopter pilot enjoying a pint in the club with his partner, Lynette Keirnan, says: “I was married to a woman from Lancashire. She was bloody weird, actually. They seem to see things differently up there. They’re very parochial and territorial.

“They eat food like barm cakes [a bread roll from the North West] and black peas,” he adds. “They feel disenfranchised, I think.”

But out on the high street, it doesn’t feel so different here from many post-industrial towns further North, with grand old Victorian buildings and the sense of better days being behind it. There’s a kebab shop and an amusement arcade now. A nail bar, a Poundstretcher and, curiously, a large reptile specialist called House of Venom.

Deeply ingrained perceptions

The land flattens out as I enter Lincolnshire, stopping briefly in Market Deeping for a scalding portion of battered fish. “Sunny days are here at last,” it says on a small blackboard inside the Market Gate Deli. Outside, a fine rain falls. An unseasonable chill hangs in the early June air.

My odyssey ends in Norfolk, where I meet arable farmer Richard Ward, 55. “Where am I?” I ask.

“You’re probably North more than anything, because that’s the North Sea,” he says, pointing to the horizon, where I can’t see anything but farmland. A few years ago, a bomb squad came to remove a load of Second World War ordnance found in the fields. “It was quite a hairy experience,” says Ward.

Do people fish out there? I ask, pointing vaguely to where the sea should be. No, he says. “It’s dead vegetation and horrible black, boggy clay soil.”

I finish my journey not far from this, by a soggy field overlooking some marshland. The sun has finally emerged. Some desultory wasps buzz above the glistening wet grass. A crow caws, a cockerel crows and my feet are becoming very wet.

The conversations I’ve had along my journey have shown that, despite our increasingly homogenised culture, perceptions of differences between Northerners and Southerners remain deeply ingrained. Perhaps we will always retain these in some form.

As Richard Collett writes in his book Along the Borders, “We carve landscapes apart to define our very sense of self and identity.”

I recognise this impulse. And I’m not going to claim it’s all grim down South, but I’ll always be Northern and proud.

The House on Otley Road by Rosa Silverman (£16.99, HQ/HarperCollins) is out now.

data.title: Burnham to nationalise Avanti West Coast
data.description:
Avanti West Coast will be nationalised from next year, the Transport Secretary has announced.

Heidi Alexander will use her speech to the Labour Party conference on Monday to outline plans to bring the rail firm into public ownership in March next year, when its contract is expected to expire.

The line, which Andy Burnham uses to travel between London and Manchester, has been beset by frequent delays and cancellations in recent years.

Since the general election two years ago, the Labour Government has been nationalising rail services across the country as contracts have ended.

Nationalisation will be supported by a plan to improve infrastructure, reduce delays and improve passenger experience, the Government said.

Avanti West Coast had the highest proportion of cancellations in Britain this summer at 12.6 per cent – double the national average.

The operator was also worst performing in terms of punctuality, with just 32 per cent of trains arriving on time.

Last month, Avanti drivers were handed a 3.6 per cent pay rise from the Government after threatening to strike, as well as a £720 bonus if they agree to work a fifth day in a given week.

Mr Burnham was one of those entitled to compensation when his train from Manchester to London was delayed in June, as he travelled south to take up his seat in Parliament before ultimately dethroning Sir Keir Starmer.

‘Passengers, not shareholders, will come first’

In a post on social media on Sunday evening, the Prime Minister wrote: “Enough is enough.

“For years, people have been expected to put up with Avanti’s cancellations, delays, overcrowding, and a service that has failed them time and time again.

“So my Labour government is bringing Avanti West Coast into public ownership at the earliest opportunity in March next year.

“That means passengers, not shareholders, will come first. More investment, fewer delays, and a renewed focus on getting the basics right.

“We’re putting essential services back in public hands and building a railway that actually works for the people who use it.”

Ms Alexander said: “For years, we’ve heard stories of Avanti underperforming, with passengers left paying the price. Enough is enough.”

“This Labour Government is committed to putting essential services back in public hands, connecting people to opportunity and delivering growth in every postcode and this move reflects that commitment,” she added.

“We will also introduce a comprehensive improvement plan, focused on delivering for passengers, not shareholders.”

Andy Mellors, the managing director of Avanti West Coast, said: “We’re proud of what we’ve achieved over the last six years – from refurbishing our Pendolino fleet and introducing our new Evero trains to running more services than ever before.

“Together, these improvements have given customers greater choice, more capacity and better connectivity, while we’ve continued to innovate to shape the future of the West Coast and wider rail industry.

“Over the coming months, we’ll work closely with the Government to ensure a seamless transition into public ownership while remaining focused on delivering for our customers and communities.”

data.title: Marks & Spencer to add Gen Z beauty ‘mecca’  Sephora to stores
data.description:
Marks & Spencer has launched a tie-up with Gen Z beauty favourite Sephora as in an effort to win over younger shoppers.

The two brands announced “Sephora at M&S” on Tuesday, with concessions in branches and online scheduled to launch in spring. Sephora concessions will appear in 100 M&S stores.

French-owned Sephora has rapidly become one of Britain’s most successful retail brands since it returned to the UK in 2022 after a nearly 18-year hiatus. It stocks a wide range of beauty and skincare brands popular with younger shoppers.

The retailer has won over younger generations through substantial investment in online campaigns, and through using AI technology to offer personalised skincare routines, “virtual makeup” try-ons and product recommendations.

Its youngest cohort of shoppers, Gen Alpha consumers born after 2010, have been nicknamed “Sephora kids”, and Marc Jacobs once described the brand as a “mecca” for cosmetics. The retailer is owned by LVMH, the French luxury group behind Louis Vuitton and Dior.

It also marks a coup for M&S in its ambition to attract a new generation of customers to help drive the growth ambitions of Stuart Machin, the chief executive. The move will also see it take on the likes of John Lewis and Boots which have both invested heavily in beauty.

While its food division is growing rapidly – with sales up 7pc in the last financial year – the non-food half of M&S, which include fashion, homeware and beauty, is still struggling to recover from last year’s devastating cyber attack.

M&S has not yet disclosed which locations will feature Sephora concessions, nor which products will be on sale through the partnership.

However, it promised a “carefully curated mix of established beauty favourites, emerging brands and exclusive products across skincare, makeup, fragrance, haircare and bodycare”.

Founded in France in 1969, Sephora previously operated in the UK but decided to close its stores in 2005 because of competition from chains such as Boots and Superdrug.

However, since returning it has put pressure on the retailers that once drove it out. The launch of Sephora’s first UK physical store in 2023 at the Westfield London shopping centre in White City was marked by three-hour queues of shoppers.

Catherine Spindler, the president of Europe & Middle East at Sephora, said: “Our UK launch has been such a huge success that we wanted to go further and faster. Our partnership with M&S is the next evolution of this strategy, introducing a retail model that complements our existing formats and allows us to build on the strength of the Sephora brand in the UK.”

John Lyttle, the managing director of beauty at M&S, said the tie-up would “sit at the heart of our future beauty offer”.

data.title: Billionaire family behind Primark nears £7bn deal for Boots
data.description:
The billionaire family behind Primark is closing in on a £7bn deal to buy Boots from its private equity owners.

The Westons are in advanced talks to buy the British pharmacy chain from Sycamore Partners, with a deal expected to be confirmed in the coming days.

The two sides have been in talks for months about a potential deal after Boots was carved off from its former parent company, Walgreens Boots Alliance.

While the sale has yet to be finalised, the Wall Street Journal reported a deal could be reached as soon as next week.

The Telegraph previously reported that an earlier bid from the Westons for Boots had been rejected after its offer for the high street chain was reduced.

The Westons, a Canadian business dynasty, are one of the world’s richest families.

The Canadian branch of the family, which is in talks with Boots, owns Loblaw, the country’s largest supermarket. The UK arm of the family, meanwhile, owns brands including Fortnum & Mason and Primark-owner Associated British Foods.

The future of Boots has been in the balance for months as Sycamore weighed a potential London listing for the chemists after buying Walgreens Boots Alliance for $24bn (£18bn) last year.

Previously, Walgreens had explored a sale of Boots in 2022.

The sale to Sycamore saw Italian billionaire Stefano Pessina, who originally helped take Boots private in 2007, reinvest in the chain as it was split into a standalone business in preparation for sale or listing.

Sycamore had previously also held talks with Sigma Healthcare, an Australian pharmacy group.

Talks between the Westons and Sycamore stalled this summer after the Iran war and the accompanying economic shocks of higher inflation and rising interest rates dented business confidence.

The Westons are also exploring plans to demerge Primark from Associated British Foods and list it separately on the London Stock Exchange.

The family were also the owners of Selfridges for more than two decades, before it was sold in 2022 for £4bn.

Boots has in recent years been forced to close hundreds of UK stores as it grapples with cost-cutting and the widespread pressures affecting high streets across Britain.

Some 1,500 UK pharmacies have been forced to close in the past decade, according to industry figures.

Boots and Sycamore declined to comment. The Weston family was also contacted for comment.

data.title: Clive Barrow, senior Telegraph sub who refined an avalanche of news stories in the days of hot metal
data.description:
Clive Barrow, who has died aged 92, was a senior journalist on The Daily Telegraph, for many years a key member of the “back-bench” subediting team which often set the nation’s news agenda in the latter days of the hot-metal era.

As deputy night editor and chief subeditor on the news pages, he was one of a group of talented production journalists at the beating heart of one of the world’s finest serious newspapers. His job, the envy and ambition of many a sub-editor in the English-speaking world, was also mind-blowingly hard, with long, long hours. And he was very good, acting as teacher, mentor and moral guide.

Clive Robert Barrow was born in Eltham, south-east London, on July 2 1934, the only child of Baden Robert “Bob” Barrow, a clerk in a glass works, and his wife Naomi, née Goosey. Bob Barrow was a talented amateur centre-forward and lifelong Tottenham Hotspur supporter who infected his son with football at an early age. Evacuated to Teignmouth at the war’s start, young Clive was brought home by his parents for safety and they lived through the Blitz just up the street from Woolwich Arsenal.

In 1945 Clive won a scholarship to Colfe’s Grammar School in Greenwich. T​here was a possibility of going to the London School of Economics, but his English teacher at Colfe’s suggested journalism and he never looked back. National Service with the RAF intervened, but he trained at the Kentish Mercury from 1955 and moved to the Liverpool Daily Post and News Chronicle before heading to Rhodesia in 1959 to sub-edit on the Bulawayo Herald.

There Barrow met a teacher for Voluntary Service Overseas, Jean Marshall. She initially preferred their mutual friend Luigi, because Barrow, though more handsome, was so rude. But Luigi owned a snake farm and often carried a sack of the creatures in his car – they would be the death of him shortly afterwards – so Barrow won the maiden, buying her a gun for protection when he returned to England first in 1961. She kept it in a box in a locked suitcase on top of a cupboard. Barrow and Jean Marshall were married in Wandsworth in 1962 and had two children, Julia and Paul. Neither is a Spurs supporter.

From 1961 Barrow worked at the Daily Express both in Manchester and London, and then had spells at The Daily Telegraph, the Daily Sketch and the Daily Mail before returning towards the end of the 1960s to the Telegraph, where his career prospered and he made the chief sub’s role his own. His kindness and decency, allied to a wicked humour and a politically incorrect stream of banter, added laughter and productivity.

Each day an avalanche of raw reports required reading, rendering down and rewriting to a hundred or so stories (50 “tops” of four paragraphs or more, and 50 “shorts”, three paragraphs at most) – composed and conducted into a symphony of print, from the tiny paragraph “marmalade-droppers” to multi-column epics. Puns, crudeness and prurience were best avoided: “Just enough to raise the ghost of a smile in the Deanery”, according to one back-bench maxim. The plain dirty was, of course, reported in plain detail, usually on Page Three.

Barrow could also be awkward and implacable, loat​hing favour-seekers and unreasoned authority. Any “Wanted Point” (a story on the wish-list of the famously autocratic managing editor Peter Eastwood) was an automatic candidate for discard on his spike. When Eastwood ordained that while the photographic plate-makers were on strike the newspaper should publish white spaces, where pictures would have been, his chief sub demurred and filled the space with extra stories in bold text and heavily ruled.

The dispute festered; Barrow was demoted to the “down-table” subbing ranks before eventually, after digital technology and extra pagination arrived, being chosen as the first editor of Telegraph Surveys and finally Special Reports, which brought niche advertising revenue with their expert coverage. But Barrow was able to impose his own high standards and balance editorial proprieties with commercial needs.

He also continued his welfare care for colleagues which won him many friends, and as a company pension trustee he worked with (owner from 1986) Conrad Black’s team in the wake of the scandal of Robert Maxwell’s missing millions to establish a properly-funded, stable and preservable scheme which solidified the less formal rights accrued under historic grace-and-favour arrangements.

Moving, as retirement approached, from Orpington to Wrotham in rural Kent, Barrow continued to help and advise friends and former workmates, another demonstration of his committed Christianity: he was a verger at St Bride’s, the Fleet Street church. Barrow’s wife Jean died in 2012, and with his children by now living in the United States he visited them and toured the Civil War battlefields: military history fascinated him. Returning from one such trip he admitted an arcane pleasure in loosing off with an AK47 assault rifle.

Clive Barrow remained a regular attender and sometime organiser at monthly editorial reunion lunches, until in 2024 failing health led him to join his son and daughter in Massachusetts.

Clive Barrow, born July 2 1934, died September 22 2026

data.title: Burnham faces backlash over Thames Water nationalisation rethink
data.description:
Andy Burnham is facing a backlash from Labour MPs after reportedly shelving plans to place Thames Water into emergency administration.

Backbenchers have urged the Prime Minister to “hold his nerve” over proposals to put the debt-laden water company into a special administration regime, a type of nationalisation.

Mr Burnham has been a fierce critic of Thames Water and has previously said it should be nationalised. He has also frequently promised to bring Britain’s utilities under greater public control.

However, officials have raised concerns about the cost of a possible administration to the taxpayer, as well as the prospect of legal challenges from rival bidders for Thames Water.

The Government is now working on whether there is a viable alternative for putting the utility into administration, with a decision unlikely for several months, according to The Times.

The prospect of Mr Burnham putting the group into administration is looking increasingly slim, according to the report.

The Government’s apparent reticence in bringing Thames into public ownership sparked a furious response from Labour backbenchers.

Jon Trickett, the MP for Normanton and Hemsworth, said: “Privatisation of water has been a disaster. It’s a natural monopoly.

“Worse still, management has proved to be less than competent. Andy Burnham should hold his nerve and stick to his promise.”

Kim Johnson, the Labour MP for Liverpool Riverside, said: “The Prime Minister’s priorities are wrong here.

“Thames Water has been a byword for failure, underinvestment and mismanagement. If we allow it to carry on failing customers with no meaningful consequences, what message does that send?

“This summer has shown just how serious the risk of water shortages is. Public ownership cannot come quick enough.”

The Treasury could face a bill of about £2bn if Thames Water is put into special administration regime, reflecting the funding the company says it needs to remain operational until the end of next year.

Any administration would allow the firm, which supplies about 16 million customers across London and southern England, to continue providing essential services while a long-term buyer was found.

Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, also urged the Prime Minister to bring the water industry into public ownership. He said: “Privatised water has ripped us off for far too long.

“Sky-high bills. Water shortages. Polluted rivers. Sewage in the sea.

“No more hesitation, no half measures – we need water in public hands now.”

Mr Burnham’s rethink is likely to be welcomed by Thames Water’s creditors, who have been scrambling to secure control of the utility with a proposed £10bn restructuring.

The company has been struggling under a £20bn debt pile and risks running out of cash as soon as October.

Its lenders lined up four new board directors on Monday as part of a potential clear-out of its existing leadership.

The proposed new board would include Mike McTighe, the Openreach chairman, Liz Barber, the former Yorkshire Water chief executive, Clive Selley, the former Openreach chief executive and Dame Bernadette Kelly, a former permanent secretary at the Department for Transport.

Under a 10-year turnaround plan, the new investors said they would take no dividends for a decade or until Thames Water returned to the stock market with a London listing.

Thames Water’s ageing network has been under renewed pressure from one of the driest summers on record.

It has been battling more than 1,000 leaks every week as the clay soil in the ground dries out and causes pipes to crack.

A government source insisted that all options were on the table amid talks with creditors.

data.title: Chinese retailers launch UK land grab
data.description:
Chinese online shopping giants have launched a warehouse land grab in the UK as they gear up for a battle with Amazon.

In the past 18 months, Chinese e-commerce companies have leased 21 warehouses in the UK with an average size of 200,000 sq ft, according to data from property consultants Knight Frank, with another seven built by investors on behalf of the online retailers.

In total, businesses such as Shein and JD.com have swooped on 6.4 million sq ft of space, equivalent to around six Wembley stadiums or roughly 11pc of the total take-up of large warehouses in Britain.

This compares with just 2.2 million sq ft – or about 4pc of all take-up – in the previous 18 months and less than 1pc before that.

The figures underscore the rapid growth of Chinese investment in vital logistics infrastructure in Europe’s most valuable online retail market.

The deal-making comes before changes to customs duty rules in 2028. These will make it more expensive for Chinese e-commerce giants – which include Shein, JD.com, TikTok Shop and Temu – to send low-value goods directly from China to customers in the UK.

The rule change has prompted them to develop Amazon-style distribution hubs to build up their UK warehouse capacity.

The race for space has triggered alarm among some China hawks, who accuse Beijing of “greedily buying up our land, market share and pricing out British producers”.

Alicia Kearns, the shadow home affairs minister, said: “While economics might not be this Labour Government’s strong point, can they really believe flooding the UK with cheap tat from Shein will help put money into British pockets?”

The land grab means Chinese businesses were the biggest foreign occupiers of UK warehouse space over the past 18 months. They have now overtaken US businesses, which accounted for 4.4 million sq ft of new space.

Nearly three quarters of the new warehouse space taken up by Chinese occupiers is by e-commerce companies or on their behalf. Most of the rest is for manufacturers.

Some of the biggest transactions included a 761,000 sq ft warehouse at Magna Park North in Leicestershire. It was leased by logistics company Bleckmann in April and will be used as a fulfilment centre for several Chinese firms.

The second biggest was a 645,000 sq ft distribution facility near Derby, leased by fast fashion giant Shein in June.

Most of the larger deals are for space in the Midlands “golden triangle” close to main motorway routes.

Chinese capital is also investing directly in facilities. Shanghai-based investor Mit-Log acquired a 540,000 sq ft development at Dove Valley Park near Derby this year for its first UK project.

Experts at Knight Frank said the rapid take-up of space reflected the new willingness of Chinese e-commerce “to take Amazon on” in a market previously dominated by the US giant.

Claire Williams, a partner at Knight Frank, said: “Chinese businesses are taking large distribution centres and building the regional and last-mile networks needed to hold inventory and fulfil orders inside Britain.”

Under current import rules, goods worth £135 or less can enter the UK without being levied any customs duty, but the relief will be abolished in October 2028 following lobbying from British retailers.

As well as growing warehouse space, JD.com – which is owned by Jingdong Group, China’s biggest retailer – has built up a UK delivery fleet, called Joy Express, that has begun operating in London.

data.title: BT blocked from offering broadband discounts
data.description:
BT has been blocked from offering rival broadband providers discounted access to its network over concerns that the plans would threaten competition.

Openreach, BT’s infrastructure division, proposed discounts of up to £9.50 per month to companies such as Vodafone, Sky and TalkTalk for using its broadband network.

It had said this would allow broadband providers to offer households value for money.

However, Ofcom has intervened to block the move, warning it was “not fair and reasonable and could harm the development of network competition”.

The regulator ruled that start-up rivals – known as “alt-nets” – would be unable to match the significant discounts while recovering their costs.

As the offer was aimed exclusively at new customers, it warned this could stymie alt-nets’ ability to grow their customer bases.

Ofcom said: “For these reasons, we consider the offer would be unfair and could harm sustainable competition, which is essential for low prices and better services in the long run, as well as helping to power the UK’s growth and productivity.”

Dozens of scrappy alt-net rivals have sprung up to challenge BT’s dominance in the broadband market by building their own full-fibre networks.

But soaring interest costs and lacklustre take-up have put many of these debt-laden companies under strain, triggering concerns about a wave of collapses across the industry.

Ofcom’s intervention comes after Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) accused BT of “choking off” competition through targeted discounts.

VMO2, which is preparing to launch its own wholesale broadband offering, described BT’s actions as a deliberate strategy to keep providers reliant on the Openreach network.

The company raised concerns about a proposal to offer third-party providers an extra £50 one-off discount in areas covered by VMO2’s network.

Ofcom opted not to block this discount, saying it was “far less substantial” and unlikely to undermine competition. A third offer capping charges for new high-speed connections was also approved.

Nexfibre, an alt-net controlled by VMO2’s parent companies Liberty Global and Telefónica, said Ofcom should have gone further.

The company said: “Openreach’s tactic of drip-feeding price changes via special offers needs to stop at a time when competition remains nascent.

“Ensuring alternative networks have the incentives to invest, grow and achieve scale will be critical to creating credible, sustainable competition.”

James Lowther, the commercial managing director at Openreach, said: “We put this offer forward in good faith to help our customers compete and deliver better value for households.

“While we continue to believe the offer would have benefited customers and competition, we’ll review the decision carefully and continue to engage constructively with Ofcom and our customers.”

data.title: Wetherspoons blames Labour tax raid for profit plunge
data.description:
The founder of Wetherspoons has blamed Labour tax rises for a £23m plunge in profits.

Sir Tim Martin, who set up the pub chain in 1979, said the Government’s tax increases had damaged the pub trade after pre-tax profits slumped from £81.4m this time last year to £58.6m in the year to July.

That is despite sales rising 5.2pc to £2.24bn, according to the group’s full-year results.

Sir Tim said: “The hospitality industry, as many commentators and companies have noted, has borne the brunt of government-led tax and regulatory cost increases, especially in the last two Budgets.

“This has resulted in pubs becoming even more expensive than supermarkets, leading to job losses, closures and high street dereliction.”

JD Wetherspoon said costs rose 5.3pc year on year, with wage increases adding £46m, repairs £31m and business rates £9m.

The Telegraph’s Save Our Pubs campaign has called for action to reduce the burden on the hospitality industry, which is suffering from steep cost increases, a mix of higher taxes and a higher minimum wage.

Labour increased employers’ National Insurance from 13.8pc to 15pc last year, while cutting the threshold at which businesses start paying it from £9,100 to £5,000.

The Government has also given English mayors and local leaders the power to introduce an overnight visitor levy, which is expected to add to the costs faced by hotels and pubs with rooms.

Sir Tim said: “It is to be hoped that the powers-that-be will refrain from any further increases, since pubs and restaurants pay around 40pc of their receipts as taxes of one sort or another – and provide immense financial support to the Treasury, as well as social support to the community.”

He has repeatedly called for VAT on hospitality to be cut from 20pc to 10pc, arguing that the higher rate charged to pubs gives supermarkets an advantage.

Despite the squeeze on profits, Wetherspoons is still expanding. It plans to open about 15 managed pubs and 15 to 20 franchised sites in the current financial year.

The company has also cut spending on its existing pubs, with total spending on new and existing sites falling from £117m to £74.2m. Investment in existing pubs more than halved from £62.5m to £26.3m, while spending on new pubs and extensions rose from £24.1m to £28.7m.

Trading has since been boosted by back-to-back heatwaves and the World Cup, with like-for-like sales rising 8.6pc in the nine weeks to Sept 27.

Sir Tim said: “Wetherspoon has made a good start to the financial year, although it is at least partially due to weather, which will inevitably revert to the norm.”

data.title: Issa brothers delay $9bn Wall Street float after market turmoil
data.description:
The billionaire Issa brothers have delayed plans for a $9bn (£6.7bn) float of their petrol station empire after turmoil in financial markets.

EG Group, now known as Cumberland Farms, was preparing to list on the US’s Nasdaq stock index this month, but the Issas and co-owner TDR Capital have shelved the plan over fears the move would make less money than expected.

Financial markets have been rocked in recent weeks by a major sell-off in bonds, which has driven up government borrowing costs and spilt over into the stock market, hurting prices.

Other companies, such as smart ring maker Oura, have also recently delayed listings because of the difficult market conditions.

As a result of the turmoil, the listing of the Issas’ petrol station empire is unlikely to take place before 2027, the Financial Times reported.

The decision raises the possibility that the group might explore a sale. It has already received some early takeover interest from Stonepeak, the infrastructure investment firm.

Alongside private equity firm TDR Capital, which owns half of the business, brothers Mohsin and Zuber Issa each have stakes of 25pc.

The Issa brothers have built one of the world’s biggest forecourt operators after buying a single petrol station in Bury, Greater Manchester, in 2001.

During the two decades that followed, they embarked on a series of acquisitions spanning Europe, the US and Australia, transforming what began as Euro Garages into a global fuel and convenience retailer.

The pair expanded their business aggressively during an era of cheap borrowing, culminating in their £6.8bn takeover of Asda alongside TDR Capital in 2021.

Mohsin Issa remains a minority shareholder in Asda, while his brother sold his stake in 2024. Zuber Issa also stepped down as co-chief executive of EG Group in 2024, although he remains a director.

The brothers acquired Cumberland Farms, a forecourt and retail business primarily based in New England, in 2019, adding it to their EG Group empire.

EG Group no longer has any petrol stations or convenience stores in the UK after it sold the majority of the portfolio to Asda. The company has been selling assets to reduce its $5.8bn debt burden before any initial public offering (IPO).

Stonepeak, EG Group and TDR Capital all declined to comment.

data.title: Octopus carves up inheritance tax fund after telecoms deal falters
data.description:
Octopus is planning to carve up its inheritance tax fund after talks about a £300m deal with TalkTalk collapsed.

Octopus Inheritance Tax Service (OITS), which has 18,000 customers, will split its fibre broadband assets from other investments, which include property and renewable energy businesses.

Erin Platts, the chief executive of Octopus Investments, said the move was about “drawing a line under” recent poor performance and would give investors “a clear way forward”.

She added: “Our responsibility is to be honest about what hasn’t worked, act on it and put OITS on a stronger footing for the future.”

The admission of troubles at the fibre division follows questions about how OITS was valuing its assets.

Octopus has faced growing scrutiny about transparency after The Telegraph revealed that savers had been bankrolling failed hospitals and care homes.

Investors faced weeks of uncertainty as Octopus pursued a deal to buy PlatformX Communications (PXC), the wholesale arm of TalkTalk.

OITS froze withdrawals while talks about the £300m deal were ongoing, saying it was “in the long-term interests of OITS and its shareholders” as the takeover would have a material impact on the fund’s value.

However, talks have effectively ground to a halt and BT is circling TalkTalk for a rescue deal.

Ms Platts said: “We know the last few years haven’t delivered the performance our investors expected and our investors have had enough uncertainty from the recent trading pause.

“Today, we’re drawing a line under that and giving them a clear way forward. We’re reopening the Octopus Inheritance Tax Service and splitting the shares of part of the fibre business, which has been the biggest drag on performance, from the wider Fern portfolio.”

OITS allows investors to lower their inheritance tax bills by investing in businesses to qualify for relief. Customers were sold shares in Fern Trading, which owns about 300 energy, property and telecoms companies.

One of the new funds will house Fern’s fibre assets, which account for a little over a third of its value. The other will contain the rest of Fern’s assets. Two classes of shares will be created to cover the new funds.

The split will allow the cash-generative part of Fern Trading’s portfolio – its non-fibre assets – to stand on its own merits while giving the fibre business the chance to execute its own strategy, Ms Platts added.

Octopus Investments entered exclusive talks to buy PXC in early August, after it offered well over what Epiris, the competing bidder, was willing to pay for the asset. Talks broke down a couple of weeks ago. At the time, Octopus told investors that the closure would “need to remain in place for a short additional period”.

Epiris, a private equity firm, or BT are believed to be more likely suitors for the business. However, nothing has formally been announced and Octopus Investments is still involved in the process, sources close to the company said.

Ms Platts said that the new structure would give Octopus the best opportunity to deliver outcomes fairly for all investors.

She added: “It’s a significant change but when something isn’t delivering for investors, you change it. Our responsibility is to be honest about what hasn’t worked, act on it, and put OITS on a stronger footing for the future.”

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: House prices fall unexpectedly as buyers brace for interest rate rises
data.description:
House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepared for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing growth of 0.2pc in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The decline confounded economists’ expectations that prices would remain steady, instead seeing the value of the average home fall to £274,251, a drop of £1,214 from August.

The rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc over the course of the year to September, the weakest rate recorded since December 2025.

The slump in house prices came with the Bank of England on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.”

Most regions of the UK suffered a slowdown in house prices ahead of expected interest rate rises.

Four regions suffered an annual drop in prices in the three months to September, with another four recording growth below 1pc.
East Anglia was the weakest performing region, with an annual decline of 0.7pc.

Traders are betting that policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4.75pc by July next year as the Iran war increases inflationary pressures on the economy.

Household energy bills rose by 4pc on Thursday after the latest Ofgem price cap came into effect. Bills are expected to jump by around a quarter in January if the conflict in the Middle East continues.

Rob Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said higher energy prices and borrowing costs would “weigh on the housing market”.

However, Budget uncertainty has also hurt the market, he said.

Mr Wood added: “We still see a risk that new Prime Minister Andy Burnham raises property taxes in the autumn Budget to plug the fiscal shortfall caused by the war in Iran.

“That would weigh on already fragile housing-market sentiment.”

Ashley Webb, senior UK economist at Capital Economics, added: “The surprise 0.2pc month-on-month fall in house prices in September increases the risk that a further rebound in mortgage rates and/or uncertainty over possible tax hikes in the Budget will crimp house price growth in the coming months by more than we expect.”
