data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Builder smashes Tudor cottage’s roof tiles and ‘steals dog’ in pay row
data.description:
When a couple hired builder James Fuller to restore their dream Tudor cottage, they hoped he would return the grade II-listed home to its former glory.

Instead, a dispute over cost and quality of work escalated to the point where he was filmed sitting on the roof hurling tiles to the ground. He also allegedly stole their dog and made death threats.

Fuller, 44, had been hired to restore the cottage in Chilham, Kent, but entered an argument with the owners after he raised the price of the renovation from £800,000 to £1.4m.

Christian Magg and his husband, Greg Taylor, terminated work with Fuller because of the costs and his alleged substandard work at the grade II-listed property, a court heard.

When Fuller realised he would not be paid, he launched a harassment campaign in which he caused more than £160,000 in damage. This included allegedly stealing their dog.

Footage shows Fuller on the roof of the house “relentlessly” throwing tiles to the floor. He could be heard shouting about needing more money.

Fuller, of Ashford, pleaded guilty to harassment without violence and two counts of criminal damage in July.

When Fuller returned to court in August, the Crown Prosecution Service said the estimated damage of between £20,000 and £30,000 was too low and that the case was to be adjourned again.

At his sentencing hearing on Sept 23, magistrates heard the estimated damage had risen to £164,000.

Josh Murphy, prosecuting, said the restoration of the cottage had initially “proceeded well”. However, there were “concerns over the quality of the work and him not attending as regularly as he could”.

After his work was terminated, the prosecutor said that there had been death threats and “sex allegations”, and alleged that Fuller had been arrested for stealing the couple’s dog.

However, the court heard Fuller had not been charged with a separate offence of stealing the animal.

Mr Murphy said the builder targeted the home on June 29, when Mr Magg saw Fuller approaching and looking angry. The prosecutor said Fuller climbed on to the roof and began removing tiles.

He said: “It was relentless, and he destroyed as many as he could. He stripped the roof back to the battens and was shouting comments about requiring more money. He destroyed most of the tiles on the roof and the roof pegs.”

Mr Murphy said as the estimated damage cost was so high, it could no longer be dealt with in the magistrates’ court. The starting point in the sentencing guidelines was a year and six months’ custody.

Summer Carty, defending, said her client had pleaded guilty at an early stage when it was estimated the damage would cost about £30,000 to repair.

She said: “[Fuller’s] now looking at prison, not a community order, and we will contest the amount of the damage there [at crown court]. It will still be a guilty plea, but not on that basis.”

Magistrates agreed to send the case to Canterbury Crown Court for sentence, and Fuller will appear there on a date to be fixed. He was granted bail until then, but must not enter Chilham or contact the owners.

In an interview with The Times in May, the couple told how they had bought the two-bed property after falling in love with its “Hansel and Gretel” charm.

They added: “For what we spent we could have had a manor house. But we were so in love with this village, we didn’t want to live in a house with a long drive behind gates.”

data.title: Lime withdraws bikes from London borough after complaints from blind residents
data.description:
Lime has removed its electric bikes from a London borough after the company’s vehicles were accused of endangering blind residents.

The company said it had stopped users from being able to hire e-bikes in Bromley, south-east London, where it was operating without an agreement.

It came after Jason Beal, a resident, said he had had to force his guide dog into a busy road because of the company’s lime green bikes being strewn over the pavement.

Councillors had also threatened to pull Lime’s bikes off the streets and charge the company for the hassle.

Liam Conlon, the area’s MP, raised the matter with Bromley council after Mr Beal contacted him to complain.

Lime’s e-bikes have become ubiquitous in London and a popular way of getting around, but the hundreds of them parked on pavements have been seen by critics as a nuisance.

The company had started offering e-bike hire in the Bromley suburb of Penge in recent weeks, despite not having local approval. 

Lime put this down to a technical issue in which the map for neighbouring Lewisham mistakenly covered parts of Bromley. Councillors said they had “blighted” local areas and caused hazards on pavements.

Simon Fawthrop, of Bromley council, said: “We have already raised concerns with Lime that they appear to be operating without our consent in part of our borough.

“Bromley council have long had misgivings about Lime Bikes and other similar bikes that are quite frankly blighting some areas, where they are strewn across pavements causing multiple hazards.

“The council has not agreed anything with Lime and we call upon them to remove their bikes from our borough forthwith.”

Mr Beal, 53, told the London Standard that bikes parked on the pavement meant he had to walk on the road and listen out for traffic, frightening Caine, his guide dog.

“There have been a number of times the Lime bikes have been parked up or propped up against the tree or left over the pavement,” he said.

“So I’ve got to make a decision to try to take him into the main road. That’s a very frightening experience for myself.”

Lime was recently valued at $1.7bn (£1.3bn) in a US initial public offering.

The company operates bikes and scooters in more than a dozen London boroughs.

It has been blighted by claims of personal injuries caused by the bikes, and said recently that it had set aside $56m for personal injury claims.

Lime apologised to Mr Beal and said that it had suspended bike hiring in the borough until it could agree an approach “with appropriate parking locations”.

data.title: Broadband merger risks pushing up prices, watchdog warns
data.description:
Virgin Media O2 (VMO2)’s £2bn takeover of a broadband rival risks pushing up prices, the watchdog has ruled.

In provisional findings published on Friday, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said a deal by Virgin Media O2’s parent companies to take control of Netomnia could lead to a “substantial lessening of competition” in the wholesale market.

The watchdog found that the deal would effectively limit competition to two providers: Virgin Media O2 and BT’s Openreach. It argued that without the takeover, rival CityFibre would probably have bought Netomnia’s holding company.

The CMA warned that reduced wholesale competition could lead to higher prices and worse service quality for consumers and businesses.

It said customers in the Midlands and the North of England would be worst affected given the location of Netomnia’s network.

The CMA is inviting feedback on its provisional findings by Oct 23, 2026, before a final decision by Dec 15, 2026.

Under the terms of the complex deal, Liberty Global and Telefónica have agreed to buy Netomnia, the UK’s second-largest alternative network (alt-net) provider covering around three million homes.

The transaction was struck through their joint venture Nexfibre, which was also backed by the French private-equity firm InfraVia.

The proposed deal marks the first major move to consolidate the fragmented alt-net market and would cement VMO2’s position as BT’s main competitor.

The combined company would control a full-fibre network reaching around eight million homes.

But the tie-up faces opposition from rival alt-net CityFibre, which has warned it would reestablish a “cosy duopoly” of BT and VMO2.

The CMA launched a fast-track in-depth investigation in July after VMO2 bosses warned delays would fuel uncertainty and threatened to pull investment in the UK.

Both Telefónica and Liberty Global also warned that a lengthy regulatory review could cause the deal’s funding to fall through.

Netomnia is one of dozens of alt-nets that sprung up to challenge the dominance of BT, the former state monopoly.

But rising interest rates and fierce competition have left many struggling under substantial debt burdens, prompting fears of a wave of collapses.

The CMA’s intervention also comes amid fraught discussions about TalkTalk’s future, as it scrambles to find a buyer to avoid a looming insolvency.

BT has emerged as an eleventh-hour suitor for the company, which is Britain’s fourth-largest broadband provider.

However, any effort by BT to take control of TalkTalk would trigger its own competition concerns and would face fierce opposition from rivals.

A Nexfibre spokesman said the CMA report “did not reflect the commercial and competitive reality” of Britain’s fibre market.

“This deal unlocks £3.5bn of international investment, which would increase consumer choice and support the faster rollout of full fibre broadband nationwide.

“Standing in the way of this deal would suggest that Britain is closing the door on international investment, further entrenching Openreach’s monopoly, and leaving consumers to pay the price.”

A CityFibre spokesman said: “The CMA is right that this proposed transaction would significantly reduce competition and risks the benefits being delivered for UK consumers: faster speeds, greater innovation and lower prices.

“After recognising that harm, it is vital that the CMA takes the next step and blocks the deal.”

data.title: Broadband start-up’s future in doubt amid debt squeeze
data.description:
One of BT’s biggest challengers is facing doubts over its future as it scrambles to refinance almost £100m of debt.

Hyperoptic, which is owned by private equity firm KKR, said it was in the “advanced stages” of negotiations to extend repayment deadlines for more than £98m in debt maturing at the end of next month.

But bosses also admitted that the company will require additional funding within the next 12 months, warning of a “material uncertainty” about its ability to stay afloat.

In a company filing, Hyperoptic said that if it could not secure additional backing within the next year, it would be forced to pause the rollout of its full-fibre network and focus resources on winning new customers.

Bosses said they were confident that the business could also shore up finances by trimming discretionary spending and implementing cost-cutting measures.

Nevertheless, the warnings underscore the precarious finances of the debt-laden company, which is one of a number of so-called “alt-nets” that have emerged to challenge the dominance of BT.

Hyperoptic, which launched in 2011, has focused on building high-speed broadband connections to blocks of flats. Its network now reaches just under two million premises and it has signed up 440,000 customers.

But like many of its rivals, Hyperoptic has been hit by surging interest costs and robust competition from incumbent BT.

Revenues grew by more than a fifth last year to £139m, driven by a rise in customer numbers, according to newly filed accounts.

However, its losses deepened to £172m from £144m the previous year as interest costs neared £100m – almost three quarters of its revenue.

Total debt rose by 12pc to top £1bn. Since the end of the year, the company has drawn down a further £44m of debt, while it increased the use of its revolving credit facility by £12m to £19m.

KKR last year injected a further £71.6m into Hyperoptic as part of a wider £150m commitment. The broadband firm has also received £150m in backing from the taxpayer-backed National Wealth Fund.

Hyperoptic said its network passed two million homes in the first half of this year and the company was on track to post profits of £110m before interest costs for 2026.

It comes amid reports that KKR is lining up Hyperoptic for a potential sale. CityFibre, which is the largest alt-net, is considered the most likely industry suitor, although it too is struggling under the weight of its own £4bn debt pile.

Britain’s broadband start-ups are bracing for a wave of consolidation as soaring build and interest costs have put many at risk of collapse.

Lenders seized control of rural alt-net firm Gigaclear earlier this year, while London-based G Network was placed into administration with debts of more than £300m.

The troubles in the alt-net market come as TalkTalk, Britain’s fourth-largest broadband provider, scrambles to find a buyer to stave off the looming threat of insolvency.

BT is now preparing a potential bid for the ailing broadband firm in a move that risks triggering an outcry from rivals over competition concerns.

A Hyperoptic spokesman said: “Hyperoptic’s 2025 results show the significant momentum in our business, with revenue, customer numbers, homes passed and EBITDA all growing strongly. This has continued into 2026, with the business on track to deliver over £110m EBITDA in the next full year.

“As the UK’s first alt-net, we are well-positioned to make the most of the infrastructure advantage we have built through fifteen years of investing in our network.”

Hyperoptic said its network passed two million homes in the first half of this year and the company was on track to post profits of £110m before interest costs for 2026.

It comes amid reports that KKR is lining up Hyperoptic for a potential sale. CityFibre, which is the largest alt-net, is considered the most likely industry suitor, although it too is struggling under the weight of its own £4bn debt pile.

Britain’s broadband start-ups are bracing for a wave of consolidation as soaring build and interest costs have put many at risk of collapse.

Lenders seized control of rural alt-net firm Gigaclear earlier this year, while London-based G Network was placed into administration with debts of more than £300m.

The troubles in the alt-net market come as TalkTalk, Britain’s fourth-largest broadband provider, scrambles to find a buyer to stave off the looming threat of insolvency.

BT is now preparing a potential bid for the ailing broadband firm in a move that risks triggering an outcry from rivals over competition concerns.

A Hyperoptic spokesman said: “Hyperoptic’s 2025 results show the significant momentum in our business, with revenue, customer numbers, homes passed and EBITDA all growing strongly. This has continued into 2026, with the business on track to deliver over £110m EBITDA in the next full year.

“As the UK’s first alt-net, we are well-positioned to make the most of the infrastructure advantage we have built through fifteen years of investing in our network.”

data.title: JCB succession settled as Lord Bamford’s younger son triumphs
data.description:
JCB’s boss has appointed his younger son as co-chairman, ending a long-running saga about who would succeed him as head of the manufacturing giant.

Lord Bamford said George Bamford, his third child, would be elevated from deputy chairman to share the reins at the digger maker and UK export powerhouse.

The Telegraph reported in May that Lord Bamford, who turns 81 next month, had chosen George, 45, as his eventual successor rather than Joseph Bamford, his elder son and presumed heir.

The tycoon confirmed the move, the first change at the top of JCB in more than 50 years, as the firm reported higher global market share in 2025 despite zero growth in demand in North America and a contraction in India.

Lord Bamford said he was naming his successor as JCB “invested heavily” in its Staffordshire headquarters and a sprawling new plant in Texas.

He said: “We have never been a company that stands still, and these investments will ensure JCB is well placed to seize the opportunities ahead. As part of that next chapter, I’m delighted that my son George will become joint chairman of JCB.”

Lord Bamford previously told The Telegraph that a succession plan was “very important” in terms of JCB “remaining a family business” and that he had one in place, adding when asked who would eventually take over: “It will be George.”

It is understood that Joseph Bamford, 48, had earlier attempted to persuade his father to give up the day-to-day running of JCB in what Lord Bamford viewed as an attempted coup.

Joseph, known as Jo, is a successful industrialist in his own right, owning bus manufacturer Wrightbus, which employs 2,500 staff in Northern Ireland, and founding hydrogen producers Ryze and Hygen Energy.

Speaking with The Telegraph in June, he said George and his father had his “full support” and that his own ambitions lay in building a global hydrogen player to match JCB’s success.

JCB is producing the world’s first hydrogen-powered diggers as part of a £100m programme and has collaborated with Jo Bamford on some projects.

Alice Bamford, Lord Bamford’s eldest child, lives in California, where she is a film producer.

JCB’s sales were flat last year at £5.7bn, while profits fell 7pc amid a slump in machine sales.

Graeme Macdonald, the company’s chief executive, said it expected moderate growth this year “despite ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”, aided by the expansion in manufacturing capacity.

JCB, which has 20,000 employees worldwide, 8,000 of them in the UK, is spending £100m at its HQ in Rocester, where it has been based since 1950.

The new factory in San Antonio, Texas, which opens next month, cost $1bn (£750m) and will be JCB’s largest in the world, employing 1,500 people.

data.title: German hard-Left calls for Axel Springer to be seized by government
data.description:
Germany’s hard-Left Die Linke party has threatened to expropriate Axel Springer, the owner of The Telegraph.

Martha Kleedörfer, a newly elected MP for Die Linke in the Berlin house of representatives, called for the German publisher to be brought into public ownership.

In a post on Instagram, she wrote “Expropriate Axel Springer”, repeating the slogan of a 1960s protest movement that sought to seize control of the company over its conservative political views.

Ms Kleedörfer also said “Rudi, we haven’t forgotten about you”, in an apparent reference to the protest movement’s leader, Rudi Dutschke, who was seriously injured when he was shot by Right-wing extremists in 1968.

The social media post suggests that Die Linke, which swept to victory in Berlin’s mayoral elections this month, may revive attempts to expropriate Axel Springer if it governs the city.

The 1960s-era student campaign targeted Axel Springer mainly because of the Right-leaning conservative views of its tabloid Bild, Germany’s most popular newspaper.

Die Linke, a pro-Palestinian, anti-capitalist party, won 25 per cent of the vote in the Berlin state election on Sept 20, and has pledged to take control of large housing companies in the capital.

The pledge was a key pillar of Die Linke’s election manifesto, which argued that expropriating 200,000 apartments would ease Berlin’s housing crisis and reduce rents. Under Germany’s constitution, private businesses can be expropriated in limited circumstances “for the public good”.

Despite winning the elections, Die Linke is struggling to form a coalition with Left-leaning parties, after a scandal over its members fraternising with Hamas supporters and gangsters.

Elif Eralp, the leader of Die Linke in Berlin, proved to be immensely popular with Berlin’s liberal voters, with some drawing comparisons to Zohran Mamdani, New York’s populist mayor.

Her flagship policy would result in 200,000 apartments in Berlin being expropriated from large private rental companies to address a housing crisis. Opponents of the plan say it would worsen the crisis in the city, where rents have increased by nearly 70 per cent in a decade, because it would deter private firms from building new homes.

Among those opposed to the proposal is Emanuel Heisenberg, a Berlin property developer.

In an interview this week, Mr Heisenberg told The Telegraph: “I am very concerned about the general effect on the housing industry. I think this will create huge chaos.

“If [large private housing companies] are expropriated at 40 to 60 per cent of their market value, it would, of course, trigger a meltdown and they would probably not invest in any capital expenditure measures or new homes for a long time.”

Axel Springer declined to comment.

data.title: Thames Water seeks £2.4bn lifeline after rescue plan stalls
data.description:
Thames Water is seeking a new multibillion-pound lifeline after rescue talks were effectively halted by political opposition.

The embattled utility company has told creditors that a further £2.4bn of emergency funding is required to keep it afloat for another year.

Without another bailout, Thames Water would again be thrown into financial turmoil.

Britain’s biggest water supplier has been surviving hand-to-mouth on monthly instalments from a £3bn rescue loan.

The cash is being provided by an army of hedge funds whose ultimate aim is to take over the business by converting their debt into ownership.

But that money is due to run out in December, and with the proposed takeover facing mounting political opposition, Thames has been forced to ask for further support, including waivers on several debt repayments due next year.

It comes as Andy Burnham steps up plans for greater state control of the water industry.

At Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool last week, the Prime Minister pledged to tear up the ban on government ownership of water companies that was brought in during Margaret Thatcher’s privatisation wave of the 1980s.

Labour said the commitment to “scrap ideological barriers” formed “part of Andy Burnham’s determination to deliver public control of the essentials of life”.

Mr Burnham has also promised to introduce new powers to allow mayors to hold water companies to account, and vowed to tighten the ban on executive bonuses.

Last month, a cross-party committee of MPs urged the Government to reject the debt-for-equity proposal from Thames Water’s creditors.

The environment, food and rural affairs (EFRA) committee said the Government should consider placing the utility into special administration, a form of temporary nationalisation.

Thames Water, which serves 16 million customers, has been operating under the threat of collapse for nearly three years after accumulating nearly £20bn of debt.

The EFRA committee said a takeover plan drawn up by a consortium of more than 100 of Thames’s creditors did not have “the interests of the public, the company or the environment at heart”.

The committee also accused the creditors of seeking to “extract immediate value from Thames Water, not steer it to long-term success”.

Alistair Carmichael, chairman of the committee, said: “We believe Thames Water can be turned around, but not by giving the keys back to the people who have been joyriding in the family car.

“The Government should reject offers from the company’s creditors in return for relief from fines for pollution and poor service.”

In response, Thames Water said it needed to be “recapitalised and put on a firm financial footing”.

The creditor group, which has called itself London & Valley Water, has spent almost a year attempting to persuade Ofwat to approve its takeover proposal.

Its last plan – worth a total of £10bn once debt and new equity is taken into account – was rejected by Emma Reynolds, the environment secretary at the time, as insufficient for customers and the environment.

The creditors are preparing to sweeten that deal in the coming weeks. The new offer is expected to include a larger debt write-down, more equity and further funds to be set aside to pay looming performance penalties.

A Thames Water spokesman said: “We have commenced discussions with our creditors and expect to launch a consent process to upsize our senior debt facility by circa £2.4bn. This would provide liquidity into Q4 2027, enabling us to keep investing record levels of capital to improve outcomes for customers and the environment.

“This is all part of process to deliver a recapitalisation of the business, as laid out in our annual report. Consistent with this, we filed a claim form with the High Court to seek extensions to certain debt maturities and related waivers that would be due in 2027.”

data.title: Nationalise Thames Water to block hedge fund takeover, MPs urge
data.description:
Andy Burnham should immediately take control of Thames Water to prevent hedge funds from seizing it, MPs have urged.

The embattled utility company faces takeover by its lenders under a £10bn rescue deal, but MPs have urged the Government to act before that happens.

Alistair Carmichael, the Liberal Democrat MP who chairs the environment select committee, said: “Thames Water’s 16 million customers have largely lost faith.

“We do not believe this opaque consortium of 100 hedge funds has the interests of the public, the company or the environment at heart.”

The committee has called on the Government to push ahead with a so-called “special administration regime”. This form of nationalisation would see officials and the water regulator, Ofwat, appoint an administrator to manage the business.

The company could then be restructured, and the Government could find a new approved buyer.

The MPs called on the Government to bring in emergency legislation to push through the administration “to draw a line under this debacle and restore stability to the sector”.

Thames is struggling under a debt pile of almost £20bn and has admitted that it faces running out of cash by the end of the year.

A group of more than 100 lenders, known as London & Valley Water, includes US hedge funds Elliott Investment Management, Silver Point and Apollo.

As part of the £10bn deal, London & Valley Water has said it will inject billions of pounds into the business to fund upgrades to Britain’s ageing water network.

It has also committed to paying out no dividends until 2035 and offered the Government a “golden share” in the business.

Mr Burnham indicated that he would explore bringing Thames into public ownership. However, Thames’s advisers have suggested that this could cost £4bn and officials have raised concerns about the cost of the process.

Mr Carmichael said the cost of placing the company into special administration would be “neutral to the taxpayer” if the investors, whom he alleged had lent money to Thames “at payday-lender rates”, were not compensated.

He called on the Government to reject any further offers from the company’s current creditors.

The MPs added that Ofwat’s current special administration rules were too vague and appeared to trigger only if the business collapsed.

They called for the public takeover to be “triggered earlier” or for “fresh legislation” to push the company into special administration.

The committee also criticised Thames’s current environmental performance and customer service.

A Thames Water spokesman said: “Turning Thames Water around will take a decade and require significant and sustained investment, but we are already making progress, and this is a different business from the one it was two years ago.

“We are delivering the biggest upgrade of our infrastructure in 150 years, and we are seeing the benefits of that investment.”

A spokesman for the lenders said: “All profits will be reinvested, and no dividends will be taken until the company is turned around and returned to the public markets. There will be no cost to the Government or taxpayers, and customers will be protected from the costs of Thames Water’s restructuring.”

data.title: Minister who privatised Thames Water blames Ofwat for crisis
data.description:
The man who launched Britain’s water privatisation has blamed the regulator, Ofwat, for the crisis engulfing Thames Water.

Lord Baker of Dorking, the former environment secretary under Margaret Thatcher, said the watchdog failed to let companies raise bills quickly enough to fund investment.

The 91-year-old, who oversaw the privatisation of Britain’s water industry in the 1980s, said he had not foreseen water companies becoming so heavily indebted or ending up in the hands of overseas infrastructure investors.

“I think it was the regulation. I think Ofwat has quite a lot to answer for,” he told Bloomberg.

Asked whether he had envisaged a company such as Thames ending up with almost £19bn of debt, Lord Baker said: “No, I certainly did not.”

His intervention comes as Labour considers whether to take control of Thames, Britain’s biggest water company, after rescue talks between its creditors and Ofwat stalled.

Thames’s lenders have proposed a £10bn restructuring that would see them inject billions of pounds to fund upgrades. The consortium, known as London & Valley Water, has also pledged not to take dividends until 2035.

MPs have urged Andy Burnham to block the deal and put Thames into special administration instead, which would give the Government control while it finds a long-term solution.

Lord Baker rejected calls to renationalise the water industry, saying privatisation was designed to free investment from the constraints of government spending.

He said there was “great sadness” that too little had been invested in water infrastructure in recent decades, and that private ownership had ultimately delivered more investment than the industry would have received under state control.

The water industry was privatised in 1989 after the Thatcher government argued that private capital was needed to modernise the country’s ageing network.

Lord Baker said the Government had backed privatisation because the department responsible for water “was always the first to have its budget cut”.

But the system is facing its biggest overhaul since privatisation. Ministers plan to scrap Ofwat and replace it with a single regulator overseeing the industry’s financial, environmental and drinking-water standards.

The Government is also considering plans for regional water boards that would give mayors and other local leaders greater influence over companies.

Thames has warned it could run out of cash by the end of the year, leaving the Government to choose between a taxpayer-backed rescue and a restructuring led by its lenders.

data.title: New home approvals plunge to lowest since 2012
data.description:
Planning approvals for new homes have plummeted to their lowest level since 2012 in a death knell for Labour’s building targets.

The number of homes getting signed off for development slumped to 51,503 between April and June, down 18pc on the first three months of the year. It is the lowest quarterly total in 14 years, according to the Home Builders Federation.

Over the year to June, councils gave permission to 237,039 homes, 8pc less than a year earlier and the lowest 12-month total since 2013.

The number of building sites of at least three homes dropped to just 5,783 – an all-time record low.

The figures show that even Andy Burnham’s new Your First Home scheme will be unable to save Labour from missing its target to build 1.5 million homes over this parliament by a wide margin.

The Prime Minister announced on Saturday that he will introduce a scheme called Your First Home that will allow buyers to purchase new builds with just a 2.5pc deposit, helped with a 20pc government-backed equity loan.

It has been hailed as a lifeline for housebuilders, which are struggling under the weight of higher taxes, rising materials inflation and mounting red tape. At the same time, higher mortgage rates have undercut buyer demand.

But analysts have warned that there will be a delay before the scheme, which is yet to be formally introduced, can meaningfully increase building rates.

Until then, the pipeline will be determined by existing planning approvals, which suggest that Labour will fail to deliver on its central manifesto promise to drive growth through a housebuilding boom.

The number of homes given sign off for development in the last 12 months was just 64pc of the number the Government said it wanted to build annually in its National Planning Policy Framework.

Neil Jefferson, the chief executive of the Home Builders Federation, said: “These figures show a housing pipeline being squeezed to historically low levels, with too few planning permissions coming forward to meet the country’s housing needs.”

Even if they are approved, many of these new properties never get built. A survey by the Local Councils Network this year found that barely half of the homes granted planning permission since 2012 have actually been finished.

The decline in approvals was led by the South East, where approvals in the first six months of the year dropped by 39pc compared with the same period in 2025.

In London, Yorkshire and the Humber and the North West, approvals fell by 30pc, 36pc and 33pc over the same period respectively.

data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”

data.title: ‘Maverick’ tycoon Dale Vince bamboozles his climate comrades
data.description:
Explaining why he donated more than £340,000 to Just Stop Oil, Dale Vince said he backed the activists’ simple demand: no new drilling for oil in the North Sea.

The controversial climate group had been waging a campaign of disruptive protests, enraging motorists by blocking traffic and throwing soup at famous artworks.

“It’s a campaign I’m completely behind,” Vince said in 2022. “We’ve got to stop the exploration and production of oil.”

Fast forward to now, however, and the green energy tycoon and Labour Party donor has executed a screeching about-turn that is leaving some of his erstwhile net zero allies scratching their heads.

He has thrown his weight behind the Rosebank and Jackdaw projects, two controversial oil and gas fields that could unlock hundreds of millions of barrels of fossil fuels off the coast of Scotland.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, he said: “We are using fossil fuels for the next couple of decades. That’s a reality. If we approach things differently, we can actually make sense of drilling the North Sea.”

Friends in the climate movement are loath to criticise the tycoon and put his recent comments down to his eccentric character and occasionally light grip on detail.

They argue Vince’s idea to give oil and gas producers fixed-price contracts will never work and therefore shouldn’t be taken seriously.

“Dale says some very interesting stuff, a lot of which we agree with and some of which we don’t; let’s put it like that,” one veteran activist says. “If you look at the conditions he attached to it, they’re never going to happen.

“So yes, the optics are not altogether helpful from our point of view. But that’s Dale. He’s a bit of a maverick.”

Another activist says: “He’s got some views that are quite out-there. But with the North Sea, this isn’t actually his argument.

“These are lines the oil and gas industry has been pushing for years; they’re not his.

“We’d argue he’s mistaken and that he doesn’t know an awful lot about it. I mean, it’s Dale Vince, isn’t it?”

A spokesman for Vince said: “Maverick is the one word of truth in this lame attempt at a character assassination.

“All of Dale’s positions are logical, and in the national interest – he pursues them with the utmost consistency, being dogged but not dogmatic.”

After speaking to activists, energy industry figures and politicians, The Telegraph found that most of Vince’s opponents were unwilling to go on the record when discussing the tycoon.

His robust approach to criticism has helped create space for a remarkable volte-face for a man who previously lamented that opening up new oil and gas fields would be a “betrayal of millions of us”.

In a sign that Vince’s influence extends beyond energy, Labour is now considering a £14bn raid on capital gains tax outlined in a Budget submission by one of its biggest donors.

The former New Age traveller, who made his fortune through renewable energy supplier Ecotricity, can appear stridently dogmatic, but is capable of unusual elasticity.

He announced he was withdrawing support for Just Stop Oil in 2023, arguing that its use of disruptive protests had become “counter-productive” and that the war would be better waged at the ballot box.

Writing in The Guardian, he said: “In order to ‘just stop oil’, first we need to just stop the Tories; to me that is simple, unarguable logic.”

Vince donated more than £6m to Labour in pursuit of this goal. Yet last year he declared that political donations should be banned, suggesting that parties should instead be publicly funded. “We should take out donor influence and clean up politics,” he said.

A spokesman denied any contradiction in this approach, saying: “[Vince] operates within the rules we have while calling for better ones.”

On energy – home turf – examining Vince’s record induces a similar feeling of whiplash. He called on the Government in September 2015 to effectively scrap the oil and gas windfall tax by controlling wholesale prices to help support domestic producers that had licences already.

“It’s time for Labour to put its arms around the North Sea and support operators with existing licences,” he told The Guardian. “Putting fossil fuels on an equal footing with renewables by giving them a stable price is the key to a just transition.”

By April this year, however, as a US war with Iran sent oil and gas prices surging higher, his position had hardened again.

“What kind of eejit calls for the scrapping of the windfall tax on runaway oil profits – in the middle of an energy crisis with oil prices running away again … seems pretty illogical to me,” he wrote on social media platform X.

It can make for a muddled message from a man who not only makes regular public declarations on energy policy, but has also been accused of holding sway over Labour’s energy policy.

This shifting picture has, however, provided plenty of fuel for Vince’s prolific emissions on social media platforms, such as LinkedIn and X.

The tycoon frequently weighs in on political issues and offers critiques of media coverage, and has enlisted the help of professionals, including flamboyant PR guru Mark Borkowski, to help fine-tune his message.

The Borkowski agency says it worked with Vince after his decision to stop supporting Just Stop Oil, adding that it sought to “place responsibility for the pivot squarely on the intransigence and divisiveness of the Conservative government”.

Vince has reportedly lined up a rescue package for the publisher behind three London newspapers – the Camden New Journal, Islington Tribune and Westminster Extra – in a move that could further boost his influence.

Vince was among a select group of supporters lined up in Downing Street to welcome Andy Burnham on his first day in office. He denies having discussed North Sea drilling with the Prime Minister.

The Telegraph understands Burnham is currently minded to approve Jackdaw, but the fate of Rosebank is still uncertain, and a decision may not come until the autumn.

Vince was also an important backer of Sir Keir Starmer, the former prime minister, before and after he swept into power in 2024 – and similarly showed he was willing to flex his beliefs then.

He insisted he was “relaxed” about Labour watering down commitments to its so-called green prosperity plan – its landmark green energy strategy – from £28bn a year to less than £5bn. The initial pledge was an “arbitrary number”, he insisted, adding that the party was simply “being practical”.

Vince’s seeming caprice nevertheless extends to Labour. Earlier this year, he told The Telegraph that Ed Miliband was “the right man in the right place at the right time”.

Three months later, he blamed the former energy secretary for the “toxification of net zero” and said he was unfit to be chancellor. John Healey, Miliband’s Cabinet colleague, was ultimately appointed to the role.

Vince went further in June by urging ministers to ditch the term “net zero”, break up the “bloated” Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) and abandon major policies, including carbon capture and heat pump subsidies.

That is despite his previous criticisms of both Sir Tony Blair and Greg Jackson, the Octopus Energy boss, for suggesting that some of the more wasteful net zero schemes should be reconsidered.

A spokesman said: “Dale is critical of billions of pounds of taxpayers’ money being spent on heat pumps, nuclear and carbon capture. That is why he has been critical of many of the spending decisions at DESNZ and most recently of the man in charge at the time, Ed Miliband.”

Vince’s position on the North Sea came with a caveat. The entrepreneur said new drilling should be approved only if the oil and gas produced is subject to price controls to make them cheaper than imported energy.

Similar to the contracts for difference provided to wind farms, this would guarantee producers a stable price but also ensure they cannot profit from short-term crises.

A spokesman for Vince argued that his approach to the North Sea had been consistent.

He said: “What he has recently done is to propose something new, something radical – price control of our own oil and gas – in the national interest.

“He has pointed out that if we did this, then the economic argument for new production in the North Sea would exist – where currently it does not.”

It’s a position that commands some support.

“If Dale Vince’s intervention helps move the debate away from ideology and towards this practical reality, then it should be welcomed,” says Russell Borthwick, the chief executive of the Aberdeen and Grampian Chamber of Commerce.

Yet it puts Vince at loggerheads with the green campaigners who are holding fast to their opposition against new drilling.

“Exploiting new North Sea oil and gas will do nothing to reduce our bills and only put us on a course to more of the extreme weather currently causing deadly heatwaves and devastating wildfires,” says Mike Childs, the head of policy at Friends of the Earth.

“It’s the nation’s continuing dependence on fossil fuels that has caused household energy bills to rocket.”

Tessa Khan, the executive director of Uplift, adds: “You only need to scratch the surface of some of the claims being made to justify new drilling to realise that they don’t stack up.

“Rosebank, like most of what’s left in the North Sea, is overwhelmingly oil for export. It will make no meaningful difference to UK energy supply and nothing to lower fuel costs.

“When the impacts of climate change are escalating – whether that’s our farmers struggling to grow food or the devastating floods in Nepal – it would be irresponsible in the extreme for this Government to cave into the demands of the oil industry and allow Rosebank.”

But as Burnham prepares to give a verdict on the future of North Sea drilling, the support of an avowed climate campaigner such as Vince may lend any reversal credibility in the eyes of Labour voters.

“If even a man who used to fund Just Stop Oil has seen the light and now backs us using our own resources in the North Sea, it is extraordinary that the Labour Party are still banning all new licences and dragging their feet on approving Rosebank and Jackdaw,” says Claire Coutinho, shadow energy secretary.

“Burnham should listen to his friend, give the go-ahead to Rosebank and Jackdaw, end the mad ban on new licences and back the North Sea.”

That is assuming, of course, that Vince doesn’t change his mind again.

data.title: Green councillors reject 550 high-rise homes to protect houseboats
data.description:
Green councillors have rejected the construction of 550 high-rise homes in London over concerns it would block the sun for nearby houseboat owners.

The proposed development at Deptford Bridge in south-east London featured eight tower blocks and stretched across both Lewisham and Greenwich councils.

However, members of Green-controlled Lewisham council’s strategic planning committee partly refused the scheme on the grounds that one 30-storey block would reduce sunlight for those living on houseboats.

Planning officers had already recommended that the development should be rejected on three grounds including incomplete planning documents, design concerns and the effect on heritage.

At a meeting last week, Green councillors on Lewisham council’s strategic planning committee added a further objection after hearing reports that it would block out sunlight for houseboats in the area.

Claire Wills, a councillor, said: “Hearing from the residents and with my knowledge of canal boats as well, I think actually the roof is often used for light.

“So there might be solar panels or things might be grown on the roof of the canal boat, for example. And because often canal boats are small, you actually use the roof more than you would use outside space in other residences.”

Matthew Kennedy, a resident on a houseboat in Deptford Creek, said: “It’s in the report, you can see the effect it will have on us, it will plunge us into darkness for most of the year.

“Nine months out of the year we’re going to be in darkness. That’s not how we live right now at all.”

It marks the latest housebuilding project in London to struggle to gain planning permission.

The dispute comes as the capital grapples with a slowdown in housebuilding.

Official figures showed that almost nine in 10 London boroughs missed government targets for new home construction last year.

The development proposed by property company RER London covered two neighbouring local authorities.

In Lewisham council, the scheme would include the construction of 548 homes across four tower blocks, with one of the buildings reaching 30 storeys.

In their report, planning officers said that while the scheme would have significant benefits to the public “including the delivery of new housing, officers conclude that these benefits are substantially outweighed by the identified heritage and urban design harm”. The developers could appeal against Lewisham council’s decision.

On the Greenwich council side of the development, 254 homes were proposed in four high-rise buildings, with the tallest at 19 storeys. The council deferred its decision on the development at a meeting last week.

A Green Party spokesman said: “The decision on the proposed development was made by Lewisham council. We can’t comment further on a live planning application.”

It is not the only time that the Greens have found themselves in the news over houseboats.

Zack Polanski, the party’s leader, was involved in a row with Labour and the Conservatives over whether he had paid council tax while living on a narrowboat in an east London marina.

Mr Polanski was ultimately cleared by an ethics inquiry looking into the complaint. He had previously apologised for the “unintentional mistake”. In his evidence to the inquiry, he said it had still not been established whether any tax was due.

Daniel Dream, a cabinet member for housing delivery at Lewisham council, said: “The council is committed to supporting the right kind of development come forward, with schemes that deliver genuinely affordable homes ... that make the area an even better place to live.”

RER London were contacted for comment.

data.title: Trump’s diesel ban would be a disaster – for Britain and the White House
data.description:
The 1973 oil embargo changed the world. In the aftermath of the Arab-Israeli Yom Kippur War, Middle Eastern oil producers imposed coordinated production cuts, turning the previously ineffective Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (Opec) cartel into a formidable economic and geopolitical force.

Within three months, oil prices had quadrupled. The Arab world’s export ban caused fuel shortages and long lines at petrol stations across oil-importing nations – not least the US, then heavily dependent on overseas crude.

Previously ubiquitous American “gas guzzlers” were quickly replaced with more fuel-efficient “compact” cars – often imported from Japan or Europe. Soaring oil prices stopped the post-war boom in its tracks, triggering inflation and economic torpor across the Western world.

In response, Gerald Ford, the US president, prohibited sales of US-produced oil overseas to preserve American supplies and stabilise domestic energy prices. The ban on US oil exports remained in place for more than four decades until the Obama administration repealed it in 2015, paving the way for the US shale revolution, which saw US oil and gas production surge.

Donald Trump threatened to go back in time last week, proposing a 90-day ban on US diesel exports.

Since February, when the US-Iran conflict began in earnest, oil prices have surged from $70 to well above $100 a barrel. Crude prices have been extremely volatile, with Iran blocking the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Gulf, ordinarily the route taken by a fifth of the world’s oil supplies.

And in recent weeks, Tehran-backed Houthi rebels have been thwarting tankers heading south from the Red Sea, undermining efforts to get Saudi crude to global markets via a route avoiding Hormuz.

Trump has regularly given assurances that this US-Iran conflict will soon end. Yet as the war has ground on, and Tehran has not only maintained its export blockades but also launched counter-strikes on oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other major Gulf energy exporters, energy prices have continued to creep up.

With rising prices for petrol, heating oil and diesel fuel featuring on US news bulletins each day, Trump is considering drastic action. With crucial midterm elections just six weeks away, which could see the Republicans lose both the House of Representatives and the Senate, “affordability” is emerging as a major issue with voters – not least the cost of motoring.

The average price for US diesel hit $6.52 a gallon last week, up 91 cents from a month ago and more than double the $2.82 a gallon this time last year. The winter heating season is looming, which increases demand for refined products similar to diesel, as does the US harvest season – with soaring diesel prices causing widespread concern.

A US diesel export ban could seriously impact the UK. Before the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia supplied roughly a fifth of the UK’s diesel. But the US is now a major supplier, accounting for around a third of Britain’s diesel imports, with imports providing some 55pc of our total diesel usage.

Back in the early 2000s, Britain’s diesel import reliance was 14pc. In the last half century, our domestic refining fleet has shrunk dramatically from 18 to four operational major crude refineries, with the UK’s heavy domestic carbon pricing and net zero regulatory costs accelerating that trend in recent years.

In the last 18 months alone, Grangemouth in Scotland and the Lindsey refinery in Lincolnshire have closed, with the owners of both plants and trade unions citing “the costs of green regulation” as a major contributing factor.

UK diesel costs around £1.98 on garage forecourts, sharply up from £1.40 in mid-2025. Industry analysts warn that Trump’s US export ban will intensify competition for diesel supplies across Continental Europe, which already relies heavily on US diesel exports, as supplies from war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia have plummeted.

As such, the UK may struggle to keep sourcing diesel from European suppliers, including the Netherlands, Sweden and Belgium. That’s why industry analysts warn Trump’s ban could see UK diesel prices surge this autumn, from just under £2 a gallon now to £2.50 or even £3 per litre.

Sharply higher UK diesel costs would be disastrous. Diesel powers road haulage, agriculture and construction, meaning price rises can quickly spread across the economy and spur broader inflation. Already at 3.1pc during the year to August, and heading for 4pc by the end of 2026, double the Bank of England’s target, inflation would surge even more if Trump’s export ban happens.

That wouldn’t only worsen Britain’s ongoing cost-of-living crisis but would further destabilise the UK’s already painfully fragile sovereign bond market. Ten-year gilt yields are now firmly above 5pc, with the Government paying far more to borrow than any other G7 nation.

Trump’s diesel export ban would expose the UK’s painful dependence on both energy imports and fickle foreign creditors. The outcome could be disastrous.

That said, I doubt this US diesel export ban will happen. The president is enduring significant pushback from “big oil” – hugely powerful energy conglomerates that stand to lose out from his proposal.

An export ban could also create a US diesel glut, leading to US-wide storage issues. That would reduce domestic production (and raise prices) for gasoline and jet fuel, further riling the US electorate.

The US produces 5.3 million barrels of diesel a day but uses just 3.6 million. An export ban makes no sense. I suspect we’ll soon witness another case, in the aftermath of stomach-churning threats from the US president, of what’s known as Taco – “Trump always chickens out”.

data.title: Britain fires up gas power stations as wind power fails to deliver
data.description:
Britain will step up generation at its gas power stations as calm and cloudy weather conditions trigger a drop in renewable energy supplies.

In a notice issued late last night, the National Energy System Operator (Neso), which manages Britain’s electricity grid, said it had told power plants to notify it of any extra megawatt capacity.

The energy operator warned that electricity supplies may be tight on Monday evening but it did not signal that Britain was at risk of imminent blackouts.

Neso’s warning comes as the UK enters a period of “dunkelflaute” conditions, the German term for still and gloomy weather that causes renewable power generation to plummet.

Figures showed that just 16pc of the UK’s electricity was generated by wind at noon on Monday, while 58pc was being produced by gas.

Kathryn Porter, an independent energy analyst, said that a period of “low wind, low solar” was contributing to the latest warning from Neso, as well as higher energy demand in the evening as the nights begin to draw in.

The energy operator’s call for additional supplies, known as an electricity margin notice, was released at 11.30pm on Sunday.

Neso said supplies were expected to be particularly tight between 4pm and 7pm on Monday and warned that a “maximum generation service may be instructed”.

This is when it calls on power plants to exceed their usual energy generation limits for a short time to increase supplies. It does not signal that blackouts are imminent or that there is not enough generation to meet current demand.

Neso also called on neighbouring countries to send additional energy and questioned whether British suppliers could take steps to reduce demand.

The energy operator issued several calls for additional energy supplies over the summer as Britain’s network grappled with a series of sweltering heatwaves and a rise in electricity usage from air conditioning units and fans.

The latest warning came as a new report from Ms Porter warns that Britain is “increasingly depending on electricity imports” when renewable energy generation falls.

The report warned that this created a “material risk to security of supply”, especially as neighbouring countries such as Norway and France often experience similar weather conditions to the UK.

The energy operator later said it had cancelled the warning after receiving additional energy capacity from suppliers. 

A spokesman for Neso said: “Market participants have successfully restored the operating margin required for this evening’s peak period. The system is operating as normal and Great Britain’s electricity supplies remain secure.”

The Department for Net Zero and Energy Security was contacted for comment.

data.title: Metal business could quit London stock market after almost a century
data.description:
One of Britain’s oldest manufacturers could quit the London stock market after nearly a century following a £1.4bn takeover offer.

Vesuvius, which has had a presence on Britain’s flagship exchange since 1930, said on Tuesday that it was “carefully evaluating” a bid from rival RHI Magnesita.

The unsolicited offer of 551p per share values the FTSE 250-listed group at £1.4bn.

Anglo-Swedish activist fund Cevian Capital, which holds a 23pc stake in Vesuvius, has backed the acquisition, although the board has yet to agree to the bid.

Vesuvius said: “The company appreciates Cevian’s commitment and engagement during this time and remains focused on the interests of and delivering maximum value for all shareholders.”

A takeover would end 96 years as a standalone company on the London Stock Exchange.

Vesuvius, which handles molten metal, was spun out of the manufacturing brand Cookson Group in 2012.

Cookson was an august name in British manufacturing, with a lineage dating back to 1704 when Isaac Cookson founded a series of metal and glass works on Tyneside.

It was first listed on the London Stock Exchange in 1930 under its original name, Goodlass Wall and Lead Industries, before rebranding as Cookson in 1982.

After a 2012 demerger, the parent entity adopted the Vesuvius name while retaining the original 1930 Cookson listing.

Vesuvius, which helped supply the Allied war effort during the Second World War, has drifted away from the UK operationally in recent years and expanded internationally.

RHI Magnesita’s bid for the group is the latest in a series of offers.

These include a 550p cash offer in March 2026 and a cash-and-shares bid in June 2026, both of which Vesuvius rejected.

RHI Magnesita has until Oct 27 to announce a firm intention to make an offer or walk away.

The potential sale follows a string of recent foreign acquisitions of UK companies.

French energy giant Engie purchased UK Power Networks for £10.5bn, while Swedish private equity firm EQT acquired Intertek Group for $14bn (£10.6bn).

Meanwhile, American asset manager Nuveen bought Schroders for $13bn and Swiss insurer Zurich took over Beazley for £8bn.

John Healey, the Chancellor, has pledged to arrest a slide in British manufacturing.

He told the Labour Party conference in Liverpool on Monday that he would usher in “a new age of industrialisation, for growth made here by British firms and British workers”.

data.title: Sewage dumped into rivers as rain overwhelms water system
data.description:
Water companies are pumping sewage into rivers as ageing wastewater systems struggle to cope with the return of rain.

Campaign group River Action said there had been 4,600 sewage spill incidents across England and Scotland in the past 48 hours as storm overflows were overwhelmed.

Sewage has been flowing into the River Derwent in Derbyshire for 15 hours, while a spill into the River Windrush in Oxfordshire has been ongoing for 13 hours.

In the UK, a sewage spill is considered legal if it happens during exceptionally heavy rain and only if the sewage is discharged through an outlet named in the water company’s permit.

The incidents in recent days follow the return of rain after weeks of drought, with thunderstorms forecast across England during the bank holiday weekend.

However, Feargal Sharkey, the musician-turned-rivers campaigner, said the level of sewage seeping into the country’s rivers reflected the poor state of Britain’s water system rather than the weather.

Mr Sharkey said: “When there’s the merest hint of rain, copious amounts of sewage are dumped into our rivers and into the water around our beaches. Yet again the profiteering and failure of our water companies to invest is exposed.”

Thames Water spilt effluent into rivers for more than 100,000 hours in 2025, despite it being a dry year.

Severn Trent Water was the only water company to receive a top rating for its environmental performance last year, but nonetheless recorded more than 30,000 spillage incidents.

Utility companies are in the middle of an investment programme meant to reduce sewage spills. Water UK, which represents Britain’s water companies, said the industry was “tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works”.

However, Mark Lloyd, the chief executive of River Action UK, said the investment was too little, too late.

“It is disgraceful that funding for new infrastructure to prevent sewage overflows – and for maintenance of existing assets – was restricted over the past 20 years,” he said.

Mr Lloyd added that the recent spillages were particularly bad, as the preceding drought meant the sewage was potentially more environmentally damaging.

He told The Telegraph: “Sewage overflows after long dry periods can be particularly damaging because there can be accumulations of concentrated sewage in the network that get flushed out into rivers that have low flows and oxygen levels, greatly increasing the impact on fish, invertebrates and other wildlife.”

Andy Burnham has pledged to assert greater control of water companies, saying this month that he was “angry” about the industry’s performance, including on pollution.

data.title: Surging Gulf oil flows may be too late to stop a ‘terrifying’ winter
data.description:
It sounds like good news.

For the first time since Donald Trump attacked Iran eight months ago, oil exports from the Persian Gulf are nearly back at pre-war levels.

This should herald a return to normality for the world’s bruised energy markets, in theory at least.

However, with a barrel of Brent still trading above $100, it seems optimism hasn’t yet fed into the markets – a worrying sign as Britain prepares for winter of soaring energy bills and possible diesel shortages.

Goldman Sachs revealed the extent of the Middle East’s oil recovery earlier this week by claiming that exports have hit 98pc.

This came after 23.3 million barrels of oil were shipped out of the region on average each day, on par with last year’s figures and at least 10 million barrels higher than in March.

The figures highlight how oil producers have effectively acclimatised to conflict in the region, either by finding ways to bypass the Strait of Hormuz or by relying on the US military for an escort.

Today, around 40pc of Gulf oil is exported without passing through the Strait, according to Kpler, compared to just 17pc before the conflict broke out.

Goldman Sachs struck an upbeat tone in a note released on Wednesday: “We estimate that the global oil market is roughly balanced in September.

“The remarkable adaptation of both Middle East supply and China import demand supports our base case that Brent prices moderate to $85 by year-end and to $80 in 2027.”

With the war in Iran still raging, this will serve as a glimmer of hope for a global economy starting to feel the strain.

Countries like Britain had been fearful of energy shortages this winter if global supplies fail to improve, threatening households with power cuts, higher interest rates and surging food prices.

This may all be avoided if Goldman’s prediction is right.

But not everyone is convinced, including oil traders who fear that hostilities between the US and Iran could escalate at any point.

“If oil exports carry on at these levels for, say, the next month, then I think we’ve got signs of optimism,” says Ashley Kelty, a research analyst at Panmure Liberum.

“Everyone wants to have good news because if you actually look at the reality of it all, you realise how terrifying this winter could be.”

Some have argued that growing oil flows out of the Middle East suggest Trump has the upper hand and is on the cusp of winning the war.

Others are less sure.

“In terms of the maritime picture, it’s clear that the Americans are enabling Gulf exports, and the blockade on Iran has had a material impact on its own exports falling to a fraction of pre-war levels,” says Darius Barik, at the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation.

“But that has come at great cost in terms of resources on the American side.”

Barik also points out that the level of Gulf oil exports can all change quickly dependent on Iran’s military appetite.

“Iran the capacity to strike regional energy infrastructure or US forces in the region,” he says. “It’s not clear that that has been diminished. Ultimately, it’s about who can absorb pressure for longer.”

He believes that many observers underestimate how much pain Tehran is willing to endure.

Importantly, allowing Gulf nations to export more oil also benefits Iran because it keeps their regional trading partners afloat, Barik adds.

“Beyond tolerating those flows, there’s a sense among the Iranian leadership that they can sustain the economic costs that come with the attritional war for longer than many might expect,” he says.

All of which paints a complex picture that has made even the most ardent oil analysts give up, with markets still racked by geopolitical confusion and uncertainty.

JP Morgan, the world’s largest investment bank, recently had to concede to clients: “For the first time since the start of the Iran conflict, we don’t have a baseline view.

“We simply don’t know how to model the endgame.”

As for the latest increase in shipments from the Middle East, this was boosted by resurgent exports from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

But analysts are still wary about whether this will ease pressure on the world’s economy.

For one, transporting oil barrels around the world has become excruciatingly expensive because of the war, fuelled by a new premium on safety.

This has propelled the tanker industry to the “highest profitability in its history”, according to analysis by Lloyd’s List.

Greg Miller, of Lloyd’s, said this was unlikely to change regardless of whether the war de-escalates.

Manny Newman, at Onyx Commodities, adds: “It’s definitely a loading problem in the Middle East. The oil is there.

“It’s able to be loaded if it can be done safely. But logistically there’s just a huge cost to doing so at the minute. That’s being baked into the prices.”

The oil trader says the unpredictability is nearing levels at the start of the war, when she and her colleagues at the most extreme stayed in the office overnight taking power naps in sleeping bags.

“It feels like we’ve reverted to March/April times in terms of what’s going on with price action, the volatility and the market’s behaviour, but that can change again very, very quickly,” she says.

Unsurprisingly, many hedge funds are looking to exploit this volatility, with some deeming prices detached from the physical market.

This is particularly relevant when it comes to current pricing, which remains high despite exports returning to normality.

The cost of a barrel of Brent crude oil rose by 4.7pc to $102 on Thursday, up from lows of just under $60 at the start of the year.

These prices reflect futures contracts one month ahead, while the actual cost of securing oil on the spot market is at $120.

Kelty warns that if anything, there is too much hope priced in.

The actual constraints on the market mean prices should be even higher, he believes.

He warns that volumes may be rising, but many countries that have depleted their stockpiles will be rushing to replenish them.

‘Demand is going to help keep prices high’

There is also concern over the fact that exports of diesel and gasoline from the Middle East are still only at 58pc of pre-war levels.

“We’ve taken what 400 million barrels out of strategic reserves so far, plus whatever China and the like have used up, which they don’t disclose,” he says.

“That demand is going to help keep prices high, because everyone’s going to say we’ve got to replenish these stores for the next time there is a falling out between Iran and somebody.

“Everyone’s so desperate for good news that they’re not looking at the reality.

“The markets are seizing on any hints of good news. It’s probably the most divorced from the physical markets I’ve seen in a long time.”

This may spell trouble for Britain this winter when gas and electricity bills are poised to hit £2,000.

Andy Burnham warned of an energy crisis in the coming months, and said the Middle East conflict still “needs to command a lot of our attention”.

One can only hope the optimists are on to something if we are to avoid a “terrifying” winter.
