data.title: Shadow bank boss accused of £1.3bn fraud blames Barclays for collapse
data.description:
The boss of a collapsed shadow bank has blamed Barclays for the lender’s failure as he fights a £1.3bn fraud claim.

Lawyers for Paresh Raja, who ran Market Financial Solutions (MFS), said Barclays’ decision to freeze MFS’s accounts in Nov 2025 was the “ultimate cause” of its collapse.

Mr Raja is fighting claims from creditors who say he received more than £408m from funds managed by MFS into personal bank accounts in the UK, Monaco, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates.

He strongly denies the allegations and has consistently maintained that there was no fraud or dishonesty.

MFS was a shadow bank, meaning it funded its loans by borrowing from banks and other lenders.

Founded in 2006, it described itself as a specialist provider of buy-to-let mortgage lending and bridging finance. It fell into administration in February, triggering allegations that at least £1.3bn had been “misappropriated” from the business.

The fraud allegations were made in a lawsuit brought by some of the shadow bank’s creditors including Barclays, Santander, Wells Fargo and Jefferies.

The lawsuit included claims that Mr Raja instructed employees to destroy documents in the weeks leading up to its collapse.

In his defence, Mr Raja claimed that Barclays’ decision to freeze payments paralysed the business, ultimately leading to its demise, and that it had never been balance-sheet insolvent nor – to Mr Raja’s knowledge – defaulted on a loan payment.

Lawyers for Mr Raja said Barclays had held roughly £145m in accounts.

They denied that he ordered any deletion of company documents, instead claiming that he had asked one of his employees to “tidy up” the business’s Dropbox folders to assist the incoming administrators.

Barclays said: “Barclays has acted at all times, and continues to act, in accordance with its legal and regulatory obligations. As MFS’s administrators have alleged, this was a fraud caused by MFS and Mr Raja.”

Mr Raja’s lawyers claimed that the £1.3bn figure was the result of flawed arithmetic, rather than based on tracing money to Mr Raja. They added that the administrators’ case failed to take into account at least £950m in value in the MFS Group.

The value referred to a portfolio of properties that administrators argued were acquired on behalf of Mr Raja. In his defence, he said that these were instead “held on trust for the MFS Group”.

FRP Advisory and Begbies Traynor have been drafted in to sell more than 250 property companies controlled by individuals with links to MFS, with the hope of raising funds to repay some of the company’s creditors.

Many of these companies are ownership vehicles for luxury flats across London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods, including Mayfair, Belgravia, Kensington, Knightsbridge, Fitzrovia, Marylebone and Nine Elms.

They range from stuccoed residences in upmarket addresses such as Berkeley Street, Grosvenor Square and Portland Place to upscale flats in modern developments.

The defence also claims that since 2022, Mr Raja had been working towards a sale or flotation and had engaged both KPMG and BDO on the matter.

A spokesman for Mr Raja said: “Paresh Raja spent 20 years building this business. The actions of Barclays destroyed it within weeks.

“Mr Raja will defend this claim all the way. He remains ready, as he always has been, to work with any officeholder whose priority is recovering value for creditors rather than running up costs in their own interests.”

BDO and KPMG were contacted for comment.

data.title: Ignore rising factory costs at your peril, Ford boss warns Labour
data.description:
Labour ignores rising energy, tax and regulatory costs “at our peril”, Ford’s UK chief has warned, amid fears of a fresh raid on business.

Lisa Brankin said the car giant’s British operations were already under heavy pressure, forcing the company to work “really hard to make sure that we keep what we’ve got”.

Speaking to The Telegraph during a tour of Ford’s Dagenham plant, she said: “I think we neglect the cost issue at our peril, if we think that new jobs will stay here irrespective of cost.”

Her comments represent the latest warning from Britain’s beleaguered automotive industry after the decision by Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) to cut 4,000 jobs and come as John Healey, the Chancellor, is reportedly mulling more tax rises to plug a hole in the public finances.

Ms Brankin pointed to recent increases to National Insurance contributions and business rates, high industrial electricity prices and the Government’s electric vehicle (EV) targets as examples of costs that were squeezing companies.

She said: “There’s a point where that comes back to bite you and I think we’re seeing the cost – the cost of energy in particular in the UK – becoming really, really challenging.

“I don’t think we’re alone in that, in terms of industry that would say.”

Ms Brankin said Ford’s UK operations would be difficult to replicate elsewhere and that its workforce was highly skilled and efficient but admitted “there are certainly cheaper places to operate”.

Ford builds some 600,000 diesel engines per year at its Dagenham plant, including for the Ranger Super Duty pickup truck and its popular Transit vans, although this represents just half of the historic site’s capacity.

It also makes crankshafts, engine blocks and cylinder heads there.

As part of an effort to secure a £900m contract from the Ministry of Defence to replace the Army’s fleet of Land Rovers, Ford has said the Dagenham plant could also supply engines for a militarised version of the Ranger.

The base chassis would be made in Thailand with final assembly and modifications taking place in Britain.

Ms Brankin suggested on Monday that the Ranger was an “off-the-peg” candidate that was cost-effective and required minimal modifications.

She added: “There’s no development required on these vehicles. They’re already in production.

“We sell Rangers around the world. We build over 300,000 every year, so it’s there and it’s ready.”

Other carmakers bidding for the contract include JLR, General Motors, Babcock, Ineos and the start-up Fering.

Ford is separately investing £380m in an upgrade of its factory in Halewood, Merseyside, where it is transitioning from making gearboxes to drive units for EVs.

‘Hoping to see change’

However, the company is lobbying the Government to relax the requirements of the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which sets targets that carmakers must meet for sales of electric cars and vans.

Ford and other carmakers have argued that the targets are too far ahead of consumer demand. If they fail to meet them, they face the prospect of hefty fines.

Asked about the effect on future investment of the mandate and rising costs, Ms Brankin replied: “Everything has an effect on how you look at the UK, which is one of the reasons we’ve been so vociferous in calling for a review of the ZEV mandate.

“Fortunately, the Government just launched its consultation, so we’re hoping to see some change there.

“We’re not looking at it in terms of our business case here, but just thinking about the viability of the business overall.”

The chief executive added: “The transition to EVs is something that we’ve bought into, that we’ve invested really heavily in.

“All we’re concerned about is the pace of change that’s being forced, and that it’s so out of kilter with customer demand, and that’s putting a lot of pressure on our business.”

The Government was approached for comment.

data.title: Kremlin seizes Nestlé’s Russian assets in new crackdown
data.description:
Nestlé said it is assessing its options after Vladimir Putin ordered the seizure of its Russian business.

The KitKat maker suggested it would take action to protect its rights after the Kremlin announced a presidential decree taking control of the Swiss company’s assets on Thursday.

It told shareholders: “The company is assessing the situation and its options.

“Nestlé is committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees.”

Russia has tightened control over foreign-owned assets since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022.

A 2023 decree signed by Putin gives Moscow the power to place ‌assets from countries it deems “unfriendly” ‌under temporary administration.

The mechanism has been used to take control ​of the Russian subsidiaries of Danone and Carlsberg.

Nestlé shares fell 1.7pc on Friday in the wake of the Kremlin’s order, which also put the Russian business of French ​supermarket group ‌Auchan into a temporary administration.

The decree also covers the Russian subsidiaries of French logistics group FM Logistic and the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain, now known as Lemana Pro.

Each company’s assets have been transferred to a company called LEV Management.

Nestlé has six factories in Russia producing coffee, pet care and infant formula.

⁠It generated sales of about 2bn Swiss francs (£1.8bn) in Russia in 2021, the last year it released figures, and has about 7,000 employees there.

Warren Ackerman, an analyst at Barclays, said the Kremlin’s order means the “risk of Nestlé losing the business looks materially higher”.

However, Jean-Philippe Bertschy of the Swiss investment bank Vontobel said he expected the financial impact to Nestlé would be small “given Russia’s limited contribution to group sales”.

He said Russia now accounted for just over 1pc of the group’s sales, down from around 2pc before the Ukraine war.

It has suspended “the vast majority of sales, non-essential imports, advertising and capital investment”, he said, while continuing to supply essential food items.

Moscow took control of French dairy company Danone’s Russian business ‌and beer company Carlsberg’s stake in a local brewer in 2023.

Danone ​was removed from the list of assets under temporary Russian state ​management in March 2024 amid reports that a Russian businessman ⁠known for his pro-war ⁠credentials planned to buy the business at a steep discount.

In December 2024, Carlsberg sold its shares in Baltika Breweries in a management buyout.

Jon Cox, a Kepler Cheuvreux analyst, said such experiences did not bode well for Nestlé.

He said: “Ultimately, Nestlé may end up losing those assets – around 2pc of its sales and cash tied up in Russia – for the foreseeable future and any compensation is unlikely to be ​an offset.”

data.title: All aboard! Princess of Wales escorts elderly to lunch on minibus
data.description:
The Princess of Wales jumped aboard a community minibus to take elderly people who live alone to a village lunch club.

The Princess, who has spoken regularly about the importance of community, went door-to-door with volunteers from the West Sussex Minibus service.

Her first stop of the morning was the tidy bungalow of Stella Drewett, 94, a former school cook.

Mrs Drewett was told of her VIP guest shortly beforehand and said: “I couldn’t quite believe it. I am quite a new member.

“It’s a great service. I used to drive myself until I decided to spare the other road users. Everyone said to me: ‘But what are you going to do now?’

“But they take me to the supermarket once a week and we go down to the village hall for the lunch club. It’s a very valuable service. It’s wonderful.”

The Princess put a reassuring hand on Mrs Drewett’s arm as she manoeuvred her walking frame along the garden path and told her: “Well done.”

She then stood behind Mrs Drewett as she climbed on board the minibus, putting her hands against her back as a precaution.

When the Princess asked about her trips out for lunch, the 94-year-old quipped that they meant “one day of not cooking”.

The Princess took a seat next to Mrs Drewett and joked about always forgetting her handbag.

“Everyone always runs after me [shouting] ‘you forgot your handbag’,” she said.

Encouraging her to put her seatbelt on, the Princess added: “I have to remind my children to put their seatbelts on too.”

All the passengers, including the Princess, were taken to Pulborough village hall for lunch and other activities.

Inside the hall, the Princess sat down at a table with Lynda Jones, 75, and discussed the washing up.

“I love washing up. I really do,” she said.

“Oh good, a volunteer!” joked another guest.

Asked whether her husband, the Prince of Wales, helped, the Princess said: “He does the drying. We are a good double act. And we get the children involved.”

Examining the food on the table, the Princess noted there was a bowl of crisps.

“I bet you never eat crisps,” Mrs Jones teased her.

“I do. I love salted,” the Princess replied, eating one as they spoke.

Sarah Broadhurst, 87, stopped by to thank the Princess for coming to Pulborough and they held hands as they chatted.

“I think it’s amazing she has come to our little place. It can be isolating so it is lovely to have a royal visit,” she said.

Outside the village hall, a small crowd had gathered after word spread about the visit, which had been kept secret.

The Princess also stopped to speak to Thea Botley, 25, with her sons Albie, 1, and Arthur, 3.

Albie held the Princess’s hand to jump off the curb.

“Look at your cool boots!” the Princess told him. “Jump? Well done. One more? Well done.”

“Sorry I’ve started something,” she laughed as Albie continued to jump as she walked off.

The Princess also said hello to Beatrix, 3, and stroked the ears of three-year old cocker spaniel Jack, as she chatted.

The Princess, who has two cocker spaniels herself, asked her: “Is he cheeky? Does he steal your food? Whenever there is cereal on the floor our doggies always eat the cereal!”

The day out was part of the Princess’s commitment to encourage real-life connection.

West Sussex Minibus is a member of the Community Transport Association, described by Kensington Palace as a “vital lifeline for people who cannot easily access public transport due to isolation, mobility challenges or financial barriers”.

The minibus service boarded by the Princess on Wednesday celebrates 50 years of service this year. It’s an all-volunteer community transport organisation supporting people living in rural West Sussex.

Established in response to the decline of rural public transport, the organisation has grown from a single volunteer-led minibus into a community transport network operating from eight village hubs, supported by 284 volunteers and a fleet of 11 minibuses.

Its fleet travels approximately 60,000 miles each year, providing around 13,000 passenger journeys.
